docs.title: DPM Expression Language (DPM-XL) Documentation
docs.text: Welcome to the comprehensive documentation for the Data Point Model Expression Language (DPM-XL), a formal language for expressing data validation and calculation requirements in regulatory reporting.

docs.title: What is DPM-XL?
docs.text:
The DPM Expression Language is a formal, business-user-friendly language that enables the specification of:

  • Data validation rules for regulatory reporting
  • Calculation formulas for derived data points
  • Data transformation operations across reporting tables
  • Cross-module validations and consistency checks

DPM-XL serves as the foundation for automated validation systems used by regulatory authorities such as EBA and EIOPA.

docs.title: 🎯 Business-Oriented
docs.text: Designed for business users who understand regulatory requirements but may not be programmers.

docs.title: ⚡ Formally Specified
docs.text: Fully formalized syntax and semantics enable automated compilation and execution.

docs.title: 🔄 Dual Representation
docs.text:
• DPM-XL: Human-readable expression language
  • DPM-ML: Machine-readable metamodel representation

docs.title: 📊 Rich Data Model
docs.text: Supports complex data structures including scalars, sets, and multi-dimensional recordsets.

docs.title: 🛡️ Robust
docs.text: Comprehensive null handling, type system, and error management.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
Here's a simple DPM-XL expression:

{tF_01.01, r0010, c0010} = {tF_01.01, r0020, c0010} + {tF_01.01, r0030, c0010}

This expression validates that the value in table F_01.01, row 0010, column 0010 equals the sum of rows 0020 and 0030 in the same column.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
The DPM-XL grammar provides the technical definition of the syntax of the language. It allows developers to build parsers for the language. It is provided in two .g4 files. The grammar uses the Extended Backus-Naur Form (EBNF)

Grammar files:

  • Lexer
  • parser

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
This is a technical document specifying the Information Model, the Data Types and other technical characteristics of the DPM Operations.

This documentation is mainly addressed to technical audiences with interest in developing engines or in having a better technical understanding of the DPM Operations. The document is not addressed to normal business users that write calculations, although it can be useful for those users with basic knowledge of information models and programming languages.

In any case, this document is complemented by the document describing the Operators used for the Operations, which should be the main reference for users writing calculations.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
EBA and EIOPA have been using for some years a semi-formal expression language for business users to write and share their data validation requirements.

The fact that is semi-formal allows automating some aspects for translating the expression into another language (e.g., XBRL Formula Link base). But because it is not completely formal, it is, by definition, not possible to create a compiler that fully automates the translation to another language or an interpreter for it.

This document, and its complementary document on the Operators, aims to provide this required formalization so that DPM Operations become fully formalized, therefore enabling the automation regarding the calculations written by EBA and EIOPA.

docs.title: DPM-XL and DPM-ML
docs.text:
The DPM Operations have two representations: As expressions, with the DPM eXpression Language (DPM-XL) and as a structured representation in the database following a metamodel (DPM Metamodel Language or DPM-ML).

The reason for having DPM-XL is that it is the language business users write and can understand. Because it is the input of all the process, it is important to keep this language formal, so that it can be translated and executed. But, at the same time, it must serve for communication, so it has to be business users friendly, implying, among others, that the Operands of the language are referred to by using rendering artifacts (tables, row, columns and sheets).

A key requirement for the DPM-XL has been that the language that is currently used should change as little as possible. So, in practice, the formalization of the language has been a reverse-engineering process, where the starting point where the validations published by the EBA and EIOPA.

The main reasons for having DPM-ML are that it is providing a structured version of the calculations, with no need to parse expressions, and that it is referring to Variables, which are stable over time, because they represent business concepts, instead of rendering objects, which change often over time and do not hold any business meaning, but just a representation.

The DPM-ML is automatically derived from the DPM-XL and, eventually, can be also derived from languages other than the DPM-XL. DPM-ML relations to languages other than DPM-XL is out of the scope for this documentation. Instead, the documentation provides details on how Operations are represented both in DPM-XL and DPM-ML. The DPM-XL and DPM-ML share the same Operators and the same information model.

docs.title: How
docs.text:
The formalization of the language has three pillars:

  1. Information model: Specifies the artifacts that the language is using.
  2. Grammar: Technical definition of the syntax of the language. Allows developers to build parsers for the language. It is provided in a separate file following the EBNF (Extended Backus-Naur form) notation (Only applicable to DPM-XL).
  3. Semantic specification: Semantics for all Operators of the language, specifying formally their constraints and behaviour.

This document deals with the information model, while the grammar and semantic specification are provided as separate documents.

The Validation and Transformation Language specification has been used as an inspiration for this specification.

docs.title: 2.1 Operations
docs.text:
classDiagram class Script class Operation class Result class Operand class Operator class LanguageArtifact class Output class Input Script *-- Operation Operation --> "1..1" Result : Produces Operation --> "0..n" Operand : Acts on Operation --> "0..n" Operator: Uses Result --|> LanguageArtifact Operand --|> LanguageArtifact Operator --> "1..1" Output : Produces Operator --> "0..n" Input : Uses Output --> Input Operand --> Input style Script fill:#0098f6 style Operation fill:#0098f6 style Result fill:#0098f6 style Operand fill:#0098f6 style Operator fill:#0098f6 style LanguageArtifact fill:#04f286 style Input fill:#0098f6 style Output fill:#0098f6

The DPM Operations serve to write Scripts, which are computer programs that constitute a run-time and are composed of Operations.

Operations are expressions that use input Operands and/or Operators to produce a result.

Expressions are finite combinations of symbols that are well-formed according to the syntactical rules of the language. Expressions compose some Operands in a certain order by means of the Operators of the language, to obtain the desired result. The symbols of the expression designate Operators, Operands, and the order of application of the Operators.

Operators specify a type of operation to be performed on some input Operands (exceptionally, there may be Operators that do not take Operands as input, e.g., an Operator to get the current time) to generate an output. The output produced by one Operator may be used as input for another Operator (i.e., Operators can be nested).

Operands are specific artifacts from the DPM Expression Language referenced in an expression as input.

The result produced by an Operation is also a specific artifact from the DPM Expression Language.

docs.title: 2.2 Language Artifacts
docs.text:

DPM Expression Language calculations can operate on and generate as results three different types of Artifacts.

docs.title: 2.2.1 Scalars
docs.text: Scalars are individual values of a certain Data Type.

docs.title: 2.2.2 Scalar Sets
docs.text: Scalar Sets are sets of Scalar values defined on the same Data Type. They are unordered and contain no duplicates. Scalar Sets are used with the in Operator, can be derived from a Component of a Recordset and combined through the Set Operators (see §13), and their cardinality is obtained with the count Operator.

docs.title: 2.2.3 Recordsets
docs.text:
classDiagram class Recordset class Records class Structure class Component class KeyComponent class FactComponent class AttributeComponent class DataType Recordset *-- Records Recordset --> Structure : Structured by Structure *-- Component Component --> DataType : Defined on KeyComponent --|> Component FactComponent --|> Component AttributeComponent --|> Component style Recordset fill:#04f286 style Records fill:#04f286 style Structure fill:#04f286 style Component fill:#04f286 style KeyComponent fill:#04f286 style FactComponent fill:#04f286 style AttributeComponent fill:#04f286 style DataType fill:#ecdc0a

Recordsets are collections of Records that share a same Structure. Technically, Recordsets are two-dimensional labelled data structures (tabular), which can be assimilated to Relational Tables or Data Frames. The columns (fields) of the Recordset are provided by the Components of its Structure. The rows of the Recordset are its composing Records.

The Structure of the Recordset is a collection of Components, which can have one of three roles: Key, Fact or Attribute. Each Component has a name, which must be unique within the Recordset. Key, Fact and Attribute Components are each defined on a single Data Type. For Fact Components, the Data Type is determined by the Data Type of the selected Variables, as described in §2.2.3.2.

Each Record of the Recordset is individually identified by the combination of the values for its Key Components.

A Recordset having no Key Components behaves like a Scalar.

A Recordset may have no records.

docs.title: 2.2.3.1 Key Components
docs.text:
classDiagram class KeyComponent class StandardKey class DpmKey class DpmXlStandardKey class DpmMlStandardKey class RowKey class ColumnKey class SheetKey class XIndexKey class YIndexKey class ZIndexKey StandardKey --|> KeyComponent DpmKey --|> KeyComponent DpmXlStandardKey --|> StandardKey DpmMlStandardKey --|> StandardKey RowKey --|> DpmXlStandardKey ColumnKey --|> DpmXlStandardKey SheetKey --|> DpmXlStandardKey XIndexKey --|> DpmMlStandardKey YIndexKey --|> DpmMlStandardKey ZIndexKey --|> DpmMlStandardKey style KeyComponent fill:#04f286 style StandardKey fill:#04f286 style DpmKey fill:#04f286 style DpmXlStandardKey fill:#04f286 style DpmMlStandardKey fill:#04f286 style RowKey fill:#04f286 style ColumnKey fill:#04f286 style SheetKey fill:#04f286 style XIndexKey fill:#04f286 style YIndexKey fill:#04f286 style ZIndexKey fill:#04f286

Key Components may be Standard or DPM. Standard Key Components are different for DPM-ML and DPM-XL, although their behaviour is the same.

Standard Key Components are common to all the Recordsets, independently on how the Variables are defined in the DPM. For each Recordset, there may be 0 or 1 occurrence of each subtype of Standard Key Component.

docs.title: 2.2.3.1.1 Standard DPM-XL Key Components
docs.text:
• Row Key: Identifies the Row Ordinate from a Report Table where the selected Variable is located. Arises in Variable Set Selections, when more than one Row for one Report Table is selected. The name for the Component is "r". It is defined on the String Data Type.
  • Column Key: Identifies the Column Ordinate from a Report Table where the selected Variable is located. Arises in Variable Set Selections, when more than one Column for one Report Table is selected. The name for the Component is "c". It is defined on the String Data Type.
  • Sheet Key: Identifies the Sheet Ordinate from a Report Table where the selected Variable is located. Arises in Variable Set Selections, when more than one Sheet for one Report Table is selected. The name for the Component is "s". It is defined on the String Data Type.

docs.title: 2.2.3.1.2 Standard DPM-ML Key Components
docs.text: Regarding the DPM-ML, the Standard Components are three indexes, which do not represent any DPM object. They just serve to make sure that the right Variables are matched together when used with an Operator. The names for these Components are "x", "y" and "z". Note that these indexes do not necessarily correspond to rows, columns, and sheets. During the conversion from DPM-XL, the values of the indexes for each Variable shall be provided according to algorithms.

docs.title: 2.2.3.1.3 DPM Key Components
docs.text:
DPM Key Components are specific to how data is defined in the DPM. Arise when Open Variables are selected, and a Recordset will have one DPM Key Component per each Key Variable associated to the selected Variables.

The name for the DPM Key Components is the Code of the Property associated to the DPM Key Variable.

docs.title: 2.2.3.1.4 Contextual Key Components
docs.text:
There are two contextual dimensions that are always latent in every Recordset:

  • refPeriod: Identifies the reference period of the data. It is defined on the Date Data Type.
  • entityID: Identifies the reporting entity. It is defined on the String Data Type.

At compile-time, refPeriod and entityID are assumed to always exist, so they can always be referenced in expressions (e.g., as the var parameter in time_shift). At runtime, whether they effectively act as Key Components depends on the input data: if the data contains multiple reference periods or entities, they become distinguishing dimensions in the Recordset.

Being Key Components, refPeriod and entityID always have a value: a Record belonging to no reference period or to no entity cannot exist. The same contextual pattern applies to a set of Attribute Components, which are nullable instead; these are described in section 2.2.3.3.1.

A Scalar in DPM-XL is a Recordset with no Key Components other than the contextual ones. Within each instance (i.e., for each combination of refPeriod and entityID), it behaves as a single value. Therefore, "scalar" means "one value per instance", which is the only meaningful scope for a calculation.

docs.title: 2.2.3.2 Fact Component
docs.text:
A Recordset has one mandatory, and only one, Fact Component. The name for the Component is "f". Its Data Type depends on the Data Type of the selected Variables.

When a selection includes Variables of the same Data Type, the Fact Component has that Data Type. When a selection includes Variables of different Data Types, the Data Type of the Fact Component is the maximum common Data Type, determined by applying implicit casting (see section 2.3.2). The implicit casting hierarchy is as follows:

  • Integer → Number → String
  • Date → String
  • Boolean → String
  • Item → String
  • Subcategory → String

The maximum common Data Type is the most specific type to which all the selected Variables can be implicitly cast. For example, if a selection includes Integer and Number Variables, the Fact Component has Data Type Number. If a selection includes Number and Boolean Variables, the Fact Component has Data Type String.

Selections resulting in implicit casting to a common Data Type should raise a warning, as the casting may cause a loss of operational capability (e.g., a Recordset cast to String cannot be used with arithmetic Operators).

If a DPM Key Variable is selected, the resulting Recordset will have the values for that Variable in the Fact Component, on top of having them in their corresponding Key Component. See example in section 2.2.4.4.

docs.title: 2.2.3.3 Attribute Components
docs.text:
Attribute Components provide additional information to the Fact value.

Attribute Components may be DPM or Contextual. Unlike Key Components, Attribute Components are nullable: they describe the Fact, they do not identify the Record.

DPM Attribute Components are specific to how data is defined in the DPM. Arise when a Variable with associated Attribute Variable is selected. A Recordset will have one DPM Attribute Component per each Property or Metric associated to any Attribute Variable associated to the selected Variables.

The name for the DPM Attribute Components is the Code of the Property associated to the DPM Attribute Variable.

docs.title: 2.2.3.3.1 Contextual Attribute Components
docs.text:
Besides those arising from the DPM, there are several contextual Attribute Components that are always latent in every Recordset. They follow the same pattern as the contextual Key Components of section 2.2.3.1.4: they are carried by the instance rather than by the individual Record, so no selection declares them, and within a single instance every Record shares the same value.

The contextual Attribute Components are:

Component Data Type Meaning baseCurrency Item The reporting currency of the instance. decimalsInteger Integer The declared precision of Integer Facts (DPM data type i). decimalsMonetary Integer The declared precision of monetary Facts (DPM data type m). decimalsPercentage Integer The declared precision of percentage Facts (DPM data type p). decimalsDecimal Integer The declared precision of plain Number Facts (DPM data type r).

At compile-time, these Attribute Components are assumed to always exist, so they can always be referenced in any expression that takes a Component as input (e.g., in the condition of where, or as the component parameter of get). At runtime, a contextual Attribute Component is added to the data structure of the Recordset only where an expression references it; where no expression references it, it need not be loaded.

Being Attribute Components, they are nullable, and this is where their treatment differs from that of the contextual Key Components. A contextual Key Component always has a value, because a Record belonging to no reference period or to no entity cannot exist. A contextual Attribute Component only describes the Fact, and may be absent: where the instance declares no value for one of them, the Component takes the value null, which propagates according to the null semantics of part 4.

Within a single instance, a contextual Attribute Component carries one value repeated across every Record. Where the Recordset spans several instances, i.e., several combinations of refPeriod and entityID, the value may vary from Record to Record, exactly as refPeriod and entityID do.

The decimals Components give the declared precision of the reported Fact, one per numeric DPM data type (see section 2.3.1), following the convention that a negative value denotes precision to the left of the decimal point: -3 means the value is accurate to thousands. They are the source of the precision used to derive the radius of a Number treated as an interval (see section 2.3), where interval arithmetics is requested. The precision is a property of the instance and is not overridden per Fact.

Some examples:

  • {tF_01.01}[where baseCurrency = [eba_CU:EUR]] restricts the Recordset to the Records belonging to instances reported in euro. Evaluated over a single instance, this keeps either every Record or none.
  • {tM_01.01}[where decimalsMonetary >= -3] keeps the monetary Facts reported at least to thousands precision.
  • {tF_01.01}[get baseCurrency] promotes the reporting currency into the Fact Component, so that it can be compared or aggregated.

docs.title: 2.2.4 Examples
docs.text: Recordsets arise from Open Variable selections or from selection of multiple Variables.

docs.title: 2.2.4.1 Closed Variable Selection
docs.text:
For instance, taking as an example EBA's Table F 01.01:

{tF_01.01, r0010, c0010}

In the context of a single instance (i.e., disregarding the "refPeriod" and the "entityID"), selects a Recordset without Key Components, which works as a Scalar with value 100.

In the context of data with multiple dates and/or entities, and supposing that the data refer to the entity with code "id123" and to the date 31/12/2020, and that it has been reported with a 1 precision (attribute):

entityID refPeriod f p id123 2020-12-31 100 1

docs.title: 2.2.4.2 Open Variable Selection
docs.text:
{tF_40.01, c0031}

Selects an Open Variable. In this illustrative example, yields a Recordset with three Records. The Recordset, in the context of a single instance, has two DPM Key Components, because the selected Variable (the one rendered in Column 0031 of Report Table F 40.01) is associated in the DPM to a Key with two Key Variables. These Key Variables are associated to Properties with codes "LIN" (rendered in Column 0011) and "TYC" (rendered in Column 0015).

The following table represents the Recordset:

LIN TYC f 123456 LEI Name 1 123456 ISIN Name 2 1111 LEI Name 3

docs.title: 2.2.4.3 Variable Set Selection
docs.text:
{tF_20.05, r0020-0030, c0010}

This case selects a set of Variables because the selection includes more than one Row. This implies that the Row Key Component applies to this Recordset. Besides, the selected Variables are associated to a Key with a single Key Variable, which is associated to a property with code "RCP".

RCP r f ES 0020 200 ES 0030 300 PT 0020 500 PT 0030 600

In this case, the Recordset for the DPM-ML would be slightly different because of the change in the Standard Key Component. Instead of the row, we would have any of the three indexes. For instance, using the x index:

RCP x f ES 1 200 ES 2 300 PT 1 500 PT 2 600

Note that the important thing for DPM-ML to be consistent is that all the Records with the same row share the same index.

docs.title: 2.2.4.4 Key Variable Selection
docs.text:
{tF_40.01, c0015}

Selects an Open Key Variable. The Recordset, in the context of a single instance, has two DPM Key Components, because the selected Variable (the one rendered in Column 0015 of Report Table F 40.01) is associated in the DPM to a Key with two Key Variables (in fact, it is part of the Key). These Key Variables are associated to Properties with codes "LIN" (rendered in Column 0011) and "TYC" (rendered in Column 0015).

The following table represents the Recordset:

LIN TYC f 123456 LEI LEI 123456 ISIN ISIN 1111 LEI LEI

Note that the resulting Recordset has the values for the type of code two times, one as Key Component and another as Fact Component. This is necessary to allow doing calculations on the Fact while keeping all the Records in the Recordset uniquely identified.

docs.title: 2.3 Data Types
docs.text:
DPM Operations data types are defined with the principle: Create only a data type if they have different behaviour to other data types with at least one Operator.

The data types are:

  • String: Sequence of alphanumeric characters of any length.
  • Number: Is a rational number of any magnitude and precision, also used as approximation of a real number. Numbers can be treated as points or as intervals. Intervals are defined as a centre plus and minus a radius (c ± r). The centre is the input value provided. The radius is calculated based on the precision of the number as 10⁻ᵖ/2. This specification does not mandate a specific representation standard for numbers. The choice of representation (e.g., IEEE 754 binary or decimal floating-point, arbitrary-precision decimals) is left to implementers, who should balance precision, performance, and the requirements of their technology stack.
  • Integer: Positive and negative integer numbers and zero. It Is a subtype of the type Number. As Number subtypes, Integers can be treated as intervals.
  • Date: Represents a time reference following ISO 8601, written as a specific date (e.g., #2022-01-15#).
  • Boolean: denotes a logical binary state, meaning either true or false.
  • Category items: A reference to the code of a Category Item.

docs.title: 2.3.1 Correspondences with DPM Data Types
docs.text:
The DPM provides a wider list of data types. This is because greater granularity in the data typology may be useful for reporting or representation purposes (e.g., a monetary amount requires a currency attribute, while a pure number does not).

For each DPM data type there is one, and only one DPM-XL Data type.

Code Name DPM-XL type i integer Integer r decimal Number s string (non empty) String b boolean Boolean t true Boolean dt date time Date d date Date e enumeration Category Items m monetary Number p percentage Number u URI String o ordinals Integer es string (including empty string) String

docs.title: 2.3.2 Casting
docs.text:
The casting between data types is possible. Casting can be done explicitly, if the cast Operator is used, or implicitly when it is allowed. The following table contains all the casting options.

String Number Integer Date Boolean Item Subcategory String Explicit Explicit Explicit Explicit Explicit Explicit Number Implicit Explicit Not possible Not possible Not possible Not possible Integer Implicit Implicit Not possible Not possible Not possible Not possible Date Implicit Not possible Not possible Not possible Not possible Not possible Boolean Implicit Not possible Not possible Not possible Not possible Not possible Item Implicit Not possible Not possible Not possible Not possible Not possible Subcategory Implicit Not possible Not possible Not possible Not possible Not possible

Although the Integer → Date cast is marked Not possible, a Date can be built from three Integers using the date(year, month, day) Operator (see §10.3). Conversely, individual Integer components of a Date can be obtained with the extraction Operators in §10.2.

docs.title: 2.4.1 Case Sensitivity
docs.text:
DPM-XL keywords are lowercase. The keywords listed in this specification (e.g., if, then, sum, where) must be written in lowercase as defined in the grammar.

Identifiers (table codes, property codes, operation names) are case insensitive: CNT, cnt, and Cnt refer to the same identifier.

docs.title: 2.4.2 Conventions to Write Scalars
docs.text:
To the effects of DPM-XL, when writing Scalars, the following conventions should be followed:

  • String: Between double quotes ("this is a string") or single quotes ('this is also a string'). Empty strings are represented as "" or ''. An empty string is a distinct String value and is not equivalent to null.
  • Number: Sequence of numeric digits. Dot (".") shall be used to separate the decimal and the integer part.
  • Integer: Sequence of numeric digits.
  • Percent: Written as an integer or decimal followed by % (e.g., 25%, 0.5%). A percent literal is stored as a Number equal to the written value divided by 100: 25% is equivalent to 0.25. There is no distinct Percent type.
  • Date: Written between hashes (#), following ISO 8601. Example: #2021-11-25#.
  • Boolean: true or false.
  • Items: An item signature between square brackets, in the format [namespace:code]. E.g., [eba_RT:x11], [eba_CU:iso_currencies]. Item signatures are assumed to be unique within a given DPM release.

docs.title: 2.4.3 Reserved Words
docs.text:
The following words are reserved in DPM-XL and cannot be used as identifiers unless escaped:

Logical operators: true, false, and, or, xor, not

Arithmetic and numeric operators: abs, exp, ln, sqrt, power, log, max, min

Aggregate operators: max_aggr, min_aggr, sum, count, avg, median, rank

Analytical (windowing) keywords: over, partition by, order by, asc, desc, data points, range, between, unbounded (reserved within the over clause)

Comparison and set operators: match, isnull, in

Set operators: set_of, union, intersect, setdiff, symdiff

Conditional operators: if, endif, then, else, nvl, filter

Clause operators: where, get, rename, to, sub, group by

Selection and assignment: with, null

Time operators: time_shift, annualise, year, semester, quarter, month, week, day, date

String operators: len

Time period codes: A, S, Q, M, W, D

Contextual identifiers: refPeriod and entityID (contextual Key Components, see section 2.2.3.1.4) and baseCurrency, decimalsInteger, decimalsMonetary, decimalsPercentage and decimalsDecimal (contextual Attribute Components, see section 2.2.3.3.1) are reserved identifiers with special meaning. They cannot be used as regular property codes or operation names.

Selection mode keywords: interval, default, the Parameter Selection scalar type names number, integer, string, date, boolean, item, and the set type names set-number, set-integer, set-string, set-date, set-boolean, set-item are reserved within selection expressions (inside {}). Outside selections, these words have no reserved meaning.

Selection prefixes: The single letters t, g, r, c, s, v, o, p are reserved as selection prefixes (table, table group, row, column, sheet, variable, operation, parameter) at the start of an identifier inside {}. An optional underscore between the prefix and the code is allowed as a cosmetic separator (tT1 ≡ t_T1). Codes that themselves start with an underscore are addressed by backtick-escaping the code, e.g. t`_meta`.

docs.title: 2.4.4 Escaping Reserved Words
docs.text:
If a DPM identifier (e.g., a property code or table code) conflicts with a reserved word, it can be escaped using backticks. For example, if a property is named sum, it can be referenced as `sum` to distinguish it from the sum operator.

Escaped identifiers are case sensitive: `Sum` and `sum` refer to different identifiers.

docs.title: 3 DPM-XL Data Selection
docs.text:
The data for the expression language is selected by referencing the DPM Cells and Key Variables of DPM Report Tables.

The references to the Cells and Key Variables are done by means of the table codes, ordinate codes and the codes of the Properties associated to the Key Variables.

The data selection is done by the interaction of the selection Operator, represented by the curly brackets symbol, and the general scope of an expression, provided by the with Operator. With this interaction, it is possible to individuate individual DPM Variables or sets of them. The actual data are referring to DPM Variables, thus making it possible to obtain the data required for the calculations.

The selection of data, together with the DPM definitions, make it possible to determine the Structure of the Recordset on compile-time.

docs.title: 3.1 Parameter Selection
docs.text:
A Parameter is an external input to an Operation: a value of a declared Data Type (or a set of such values) that is provided as input to the runtime alongside the data instances. Using a Parameter in an Operation therefore implies that the execution environment must supply a value for the Parameter together with the data instances; otherwise, the Parameter takes its declared default (or null when no default is declared).

Parameters let the same Operation be reused across executions that differ only in a threshold, a reference date, an enumeration member, an allowed set of codes, or any other configuration value that is not stored in the Cells of the input tables.

Parameters are referenced using the selection Operator with the p prefix, followed by the declared Data Type, and optionally followed by a default value.

docs.title: 3.1.1 Syntax
docs.text:
{ p[]parameter, type [, _default_value] }

where:

  • parameter is the parameter code, following the same conventions as a Variable code. As with the other selection prefixes, an optional underscore between p and the code is allowed as a cosmetic separator: pthreshold and p_threshold refer to the same Parameter. To reference a code that itself starts with an underscore, backtick-escape the code (e.g. p`_legacy_param`).
  • type is the declared Data Type of the Parameter. Allowed values:
    • Scalar types: number, integer, string, date, boolean, item.
    • Set types: set-number, set-integer, set-string, set-date, set-boolean, set-item — a Set parameter takes a set of values of the corresponding Scalar type at execution time.
  • default_value is an optional default, written as default: <literal> for Scalar types, default: [namespace:code] for parameters of type item, or default: { <literal>, ... } / default: { [ns:c], ... } for Set types. When omitted, the implicit default is null.

docs.title: 3.1.2 Semantics
docs.text:
A Parameter Selection evaluates to a Scalar (for the basic types) or a set value (for the set-* types), of the declared Data Type. The value is supplied by the execution environment at run time, as part of the input alongside the data instances. If no value is supplied:

  • if a default is declared in the selection, the Parameter takes the default value;
  • otherwise, the Parameter is null.

The declared type fixes the Data Type of the resulting value and is used at compile time to check that the Parameter is used in a position compatible with its type (e.g. an integer Parameter cannot be passed where a date is required, unless an explicit cast is applied; a set-item Parameter can be used as the right-hand side of an in Operator, but not where a Scalar is expected).

docs.title: 3.1.3 Additional Constraints
docs.text:
• The default value, when provided, must be compatible with the declared Data Type: an integer Parameter accepts an integer literal default; a date Parameter accepts a date literal default; an item Parameter accepts an item reference default; a set-<type> Parameter accepts a set literal whose elements are of <type>.
  • The declared Data Type must be one of the twelve listed above. Number Interval, Subcategory and Recordset-shaped Parameters are not supported by this syntax.

docs.title: 3.1.4 Runtime Binding
docs.text: Because a Parameter is not part of the data instances, using a Parameter in an Operation changes the contract between the Operation and its execution environment: the engine must accept the bindings for every Parameter referenced by the Operation (and by any other Operation it transitively depends on), in addition to the usual data instances. How those bindings are delivered (configuration file, command-line argument, REST parameter, etc.) is left to the implementer; this specification only requires that the engine resolve each Parameter code to a value of the declared type at evaluation time, falling back to the declared default — or to null — when no binding is supplied.

docs.title: 3.1.5 Examples
docs.text:
Declaring a Parameter with no default — evaluates to null if no binding is supplied at runtime:

{p_threshold, number}

Declaring a Parameter with an explicit default:

{p_threshold, number, default: 0}
{p_cutoff, date, default: #2025-01-01#}
{p_ccy, item, default: [eba_CU:EUR]}

Using a Parameter in an Operation — the same expression can be re-executed against different thresholds without modifying the DPM:

{tT1, r010, c010} > {p_threshold, number, default: 0}

Using a Parameter inside a where clause to filter Records by an externally-supplied reference date:

{tT1}[where refPeriod >= {p_cutoff, date}]

Using an Item-typed Parameter with a default — filters Records by currency, defaulting to EUR when no binding is supplied:

{tT1}[where ccy = {p_ccy, item, default: [eba_CU:EUR]}]

Declaring a Set Parameter and using it as the right-hand side of in — the runtime supplies the set of allowed currencies, falling back to a single-element default when unbound:

{tT1}[where ccy in {p_ccys, set-item, default: {[eba_CU:EUR]}}]

Referencing a parameter whose code starts with an underscore via backtick escaping:

{p`_legacy_param`, number}

docs.title: 4.1 Null and Data Types
docs.text: All the Data Types are assumed to contain the conventional value null, which means "no value", or "absence of known value" or "missing value". Note that the null value, therefore, is the only value of multiple different types.

docs.title: 4.2 Implicit and Explicit Null Values
docs.text:
For Recordsets, nulls may arise in a selection for two reasons:

  • Explicit null: In the input data for the engine, there is a Record without a value.
  • Implicit null: In the input data for the engine, there is no Record for one of the Variables in the selection. In this case, the engine will generate a Record for that Variable with a null value, or another specified default (see Selection Operator in part 2).

In any case, there are no differences in how implicit or explicit nulls are treated.

docs.title: 4.2.1 Implicit Nulls Generation
docs.text:
Generation of implicit nulls is necessary because of the default values. Whenever a set of Variables is selected, all the selected Variables need to be created, even if they have not been reported (implicit null).

For closed tables, one Record shall be generated for each variable in the selection.

For open tables, for each combination of Keys that has at least one value reported (including explicit nulls), one Record for each non existing Variable shall be generated.

docs.title: 4.3 Null Treatment
docs.text:
In general, most of the Operations return null when any of their arguments is null.

  • Comparison Operators (e.g., =, >): if a null is involved in the operation, then the result is null.
  • Arithmetic Operators (e.g., + , -, *): if a null is involved in the operation, then the result is null.
  • String Operators: if a null is involved in the operation, then the result is null.
  • Logical Operators (and, or, xor, not): Three-value logic is adopted with the consideration that null means unknown. The concrete results for each Operator are specified in part 2, in the description of the Operators.
  • Conditional Operators: null is considered equivalent to false.
  • Filtering: null is considered equivalent to false (i.e., the Records with a null value are not selected in the filter).
  • Aggregations (e.g., sum, avg, max): nulls are excluded from the calculations. If all input values are null, the result is null. The exception is count, which returns 0 in that case and never returns null.
  • Intervals: If the centre is null, the radius is also null.

docs.title: 4.4 Overriding the Standard Null Treatment
docs.text:
The standard null treatment can be overridden by substituting the null values for other values. This can be done in two ways:

  • With the Selection Operator: It is possible to set a default value in the selection for the null values.
  • With the nvl Operator: serves to substitute nulls for any value.

docs.title: 5.1 Operation and OperationVersion
docs.text:
Operations have a code and can be grouped.

Groups of Operations refer to the cases where users define a parent validation and the system derives automatically children validations. There can only be two levels of Operations (i.e., a child validation cannot be the parent of another validation). The types of validations that generate children are Variant and Property constraint validations (see below).

Operations and may be of any of 4 types:

  • Validation: Operations that serve to validate the consistency of data. They can provide as output a Scalar Boolean value or a Recordset with Scalar values.
  • Calculation: Operations that serve to derive new data. They can provide as output any kind of data.
  • Precondition: Operations that serve to determine whether one or more validations shall be applied. They can only provide as output a Scalar Boolean value.
  • Conditional_severity: Operations that serve to determine the severity of an invalid result for a validation. It can yield a value 'error' or 'warning'

Operations are also classified based on their source for generation as:

  • User_defined: Operations that have been defined by users.
  • Hierarchy: Validations that have been automatically generated by the system based on the contents of subhierarchies.
  • Sign: Validations that have been automatically generated by the system based on the contents of the Sign attribute for TableVersionCells.
  • Existence: Validations that have been automatically generated by the system based on the IsNullable attribute for TableVersionCells.
  • Variant: Validations that are defined at the level of TableGroups, including the individual validations generated from them.
  • Property_constraint: Validations that are defined at the level of a property, and from which individual instances of validations based on Variables are generated.

Operations can have many versions. A new version of an Operation is required whenever any of the following attributes change:

  • Expression: The DPM-XL expression of the version.
  • Description: Natural language description of what the validation is aimed to check.
  • PreconditionOperation: A link to an Operation version that acts as precondition.
  • SeverityOperation: A link to an Operation that determines the conditional severity.

docs.title: 5.2.1 Operation Nodes
docs.text:
The tree representation of an OperationVersion is provided in the OperationNode table.

Any Operation can be represented as a hierarchical tree, where the arguments of one Operator are represented.

For instance, the expression:

A = B + C

Can be represented as:

    =
   / \
  A   +
     / \
    B   C

Where "=" and "+" are Operators, and "A", "B" and "C" are Operands.

This kind of tree is represented in the OperationNode table.

docs.title: 5.2.2 Operands' Representation
docs.text:
All Operands are represented as OperationNodes.

Operands that are Scalars not representing a DPM Object (like an Item) are completely represented in the OperationNode table.

Scalar Operands that are referring to a DPM Object need to be further specified with the tables OperandSource and OperandReference, which provide the reference to the DPM Object.

Operands that are Variables and Sets of Variables need also to be further specified with the tables OperandSource and OperandReference. Concretely, for Sets of Variables, it is important to determine the index of each Variable in the context of the Operand, to be able to match the Variables to which the Operator applies.

docs.title: 5.2.3 Representation Example
docs.text:
For instance, suppose a table (Tab1) with three rows (100, 200 and 300), two columns (100 and 200) and two sheets.

Sheet A

Column 100 Column 200 Row 100 1 4 Row 200 2 5 Row 300 3 6

Sheet B

Column 100 Column 200 Row 100 7 10 Row 200 8 11 Row 300 9 12

Note that each number in the cells represents the ID of the corresponding Variable.

The following expression:

{tTab1, r100, c*, s*} = 2 * ({tTab1, r200, c*, s*} + {tTab1, r300, c*, s*})

Would be represented as the following tree:

             =
           /   \
{tTab1, r100, c*, s*}   *
                       / \
                      2   +
                         / \
           {tTab1, r200, c*, s*} {tTab1, r300, c*, s*}

The representation in the DB would be as follows (only the relevant fields are shown, and for Operators and argument symbols are used):

OperationNode Table

NodeId ParentNodeID Operator Argument OperandSourceId Scalar 1 = 2 1 left oprnd1 3 1 * right 4 3 left 2 5 3 + right 6 5 left oprnd2 7 5 right oprnd3

OperandReference Table

The x, y and z columns hold the index of the Variable on the row, column and sheet axis respectively. In this expression the row is fixed on each Operand, so x is not used; the column and sheet axes vary, and are indexed by y and z.

NodeID x y z VariableID 2 1 1 1 2 2 1 4 2 1 2 7 2 2 2 10 6 1 1 2 6 2 1 5 6 1 2 8 6 2 2 11 7 1 1 3 7 2 1 6 7 1 2 9 7 2 2 12

Note that the Operations shall be applied to the Variables having the same index. For instance, Variable 1 = 2 * (Variable 2 + Variable 3), because all of them have the index y=1 and z=1.

docs.title: 5.3 Operation Scope
docs.text:
Each Operation version can be applied in different scopes. An Operation scope refers to the individual module versions or sets of module versions (for cross-module validations) to which the Operation logically applies.

For each Operation scope, there may be different values for the attributes:

  • IsActive: Determines whether the Operation shall be run for a certain scope.
  • Severity: Determines the severity of the error, if the validation is not passed.
  • FromSubmissionDate: Sets a date from which the validation applies to subsequent submissions.

docs.title: 5.4 Variable Calculation
docs.text: For calculations (i.e., Operations that serve to calculate values for Variables), it is necessary to link the Operation to the actual Variable that is generated. This is done with the VariableCalculation table, which links to the Variable and the Module. The link to the Module is necessary due to the fact that a Variable can be used in several Modules, being calculated in some cases and not calculated in other cases.

docs.title: 1 Introduction
docs.text:
This documentation provides the individual description of the semantics for all the Operators in the DPM Operations (DPM-XL and DPM-ML).

The document is structured from more generic to more concrete. It starts with general behaviours that apply to several Operators of different types. Then it follows with the common behaviour of the Operators of the same type, finalizing with the specific behaviour of the single Operators.

docs.title: 1.1 Operator Precedence
docs.text:
The table below lists operator precedence from lowest (level 1) to highest (level 12), derived from the order of alternatives in the grammar's expression rule. Operators at higher levels bind more tightly. When operators share a level they associate left-to-right. Use parentheses () to override any precedence.

Level Operator(s) Category 1 or, xor Logical disjunction 2 and Logical conjunction 3 in Set membership 4 =, <>, <, >, <=, >= Comparison 5 \|\| String concatenation 6 +, - Additive 7 *, / Multiplicative 8 not(...) Logical negation 9 +, - (unary) Unary sign 10 [where ...], [sub ...], [rename ...], [get ...] Clause operators (postfix) 11 Function calls, literals, selections, item references Atomic expressions 12 (...) Parenthesised grouping

if … then … else … endif encloses a full expression and is always evaluated as a unit; its precedence is that of the enclosed expressions.

This ordering mirrors the precedence structure of VTL (Validation and Transformation Language), which DPM-XL is based on.

docs.title: 2 Common General Behaviours for the Operators
2.1 Unary Operators
docs.text:
This general behaviour is applied to Operators taking as an argument one single Operand.

Unless explicitly specified differently, the behaviour for the unary Operators is as follows:

docs.title: 2.1.1 Scalars
docs.text: The Operator is applied on a Scalar value and returns a Scalar value.

docs.title: 2.1.2 Recordsets
docs.text:
The Operator is applied on a Recordset and returns a Recordset.

The Operator is applied to the values of all the facts of the Recordset.

docs.title: 2.1.2.1 Constraints
docs.text: 1. The Data Type of the Fact Component of the Operand Recordset must be compatible with the Operator.

docs.title: 2.1.2.2 Structure
docs.text: The structure of the resulting Recordset contains the Key and Fact Components of the Operand Recordset, the Attribute Components are not propagated.

docs.title: 2.1.2.3 Records
docs.text:
The Operators produce one output Record per each input Record, which have:

  • For Key Components, the values unchanged.
  • For the Fact values, the Operator is applied to the input value and returns the corresponding value.

docs.title: 2.2 Binary Operators
docs.text:
This general behaviour is applied whenever an Operator takes as input two Operands, which includes the following Operators:

  • Arithmetic Binary Operators
  • Comparison Operators
  • Logical Binary Operators

Unless explicitly specified differently, the behaviour for the binary Operators is as follows.

docs.title: 2.2.1 Scalars
docs.text: If the two Operands of a binary Operator are Scalars, the result shall be the Scalar resulting of applying the Operator to the Operands.

docs.title: 2.2.2 Recordset and Scalar
docs.text: A binary Operator applied to a Recordset Operand and a Scalar, will result in a Recordset with the same Key and Fact Components as the input Recordset Operand (Attribute Components are not propagated). The Operator shall be applied to every Record of the input Recordset and the Scalar.

docs.title: 2.2.2.1 Examples
docs.text:
0.25*{tS_26.01, r0600, cNNN}

Supposing that the selection yields the following Recordset:

c f 0060 100 0080 200

The operation results in:

c f 0060 25 0080 50

docs.title: 2.2.3.1 Constraints
docs.text:
Binary Operators can only be applied to two Recordsets Operands if they have:

  1. exactly the same Key Components; or
  2. the Key Components of one Recordset (Reference Recordset) are a superset of the Key Components of the other Recordset.
  3. Standard Keys contain the same values. E.g., summing {tT1, r010-020} and {tT1, r030-040} is not possible, because there are no matches in the operands.

docs.title: 2.2.3.2 Structure
docs.text: The Operator yields a Recordset with the common Key Components in case 1, or the Key Components of the Reference Recordset in case 2. The resulting Recordset does not contain any Attribute Component from the Operand Recordsets.

docs.title: 2.2.3.3 Records
docs.text: The Operator applies to the pairs of values resulting from performing an inner join of the input Recordsets on the common Key Components.

docs.title: 2.2.3.4.2 Subset of Identifiers
docs.text:
{tF_40.01, c0110} >= {tF_40.02, c0060}

Supposing that the selections yield:

{tF_40.01, c0110}

LIN TYC f 123 x1 1 456 x1 0.8 789 x1 0.4

{tF_40.02, c0060}

LIN TYC STC LHC LHO f 123 x1 111 ABC x1 0.3 123 x1 111 DEF x1 0.7 456 x1 222 ABC x1 0.85

The result would be:

LIN TYC STC LHC LHO f 123 x1 111 ABC x1 true 123 x1 111 DEF x1 true 456 x1 222 ABC x1 false

Note that:

  • An inner join on the common Key Components is performed. This means that there is no comparison for the Record in F 40.01 with LIN = 789, because there is no match in F 40.02.
  • The result of the operation has the Structure of the Reference Recordset, which is the one that has a superset of Key Components.
  • For each match in the join the Operator >= is applied to the pairs of values for the facts.

docs.title: 2.2.4 Intervals Treatment
docs.text: When one of two numeric Operands is an interval, and the other is a point, the point is transformed into an interval with centre value equal to the point value, and radius 0.

docs.title: 3.1.1 Syntax
docs.text:
All selection forms use a single-letter prefix (t, g, v, o, p) followed by an identifier code. An optional underscore between the prefix and the code is allowed as a cosmetic separator for readability: tT1 and t_T1 refer to the same table, vfoo and v_foo refer to the same Variable, etc.

Form 1 — Table reference

{ t[]table [, rrow_args] [, ccol_args] [, ssheet_args] [, _interval_arithmetics] [, default_value] }

Form 2 — Table group reference

{ g[]table_group [, rrow_args] [, ccol_args] [, ssheet_args] [, _interval_arithmetics] [, default_value] }

Form 3 — Variable reference

{ v[_]variable }

No row, column, sheet, or other arguments are permitted.

Form 4 — Operation reference

{ o[_]operation [, rrow_args] [, ccol_args] [, ssheet_args] }

Form 5 — Parameter reference

{ p[]parameter, type [, _default_value] }

A Parameter is an execution-time value of a declared Data Type — either a Scalar (for the basic types) or a set of values (for the set-* types) — supplied as input to the runtime alongside the data instances. See §3.1 Parameter Selection for the full specification. Unlike Forms 1–4, a Parameter Selection produces a Scalar or a set, not a Recordset.

Escaping codes with leading underscores or other special characters

A code that starts with an underscore (or contains characters not allowed in the bare code) can be referenced by backtick-escaping the code part after the prefix:

{ v`_internal` } — selects the Variable whose code is _internal.

{ t`_meta` } — selects the table whose code is _meta.

The escape applies only to the code; the prefix stays outside the backticks. Without escaping, codes must start with a letter.

where row_args, col_args, and sheet_args follow the pattern:

rrow [, rrow]* | rrow_init–row_end | r*

ccol [, ccol]* | ccol_init–col_end | c*

ssheet [, ssheet]* | ssheet_init–sheet_end | s*

docs.title: 3.1.2 Input Parameters
docs.text:
• table: The code of a DPM Report table.
  • variable: the code of a DPM Variable.
  • operation: The code of a DPM Operation.
  • row, row_init, row_end: A Reference to the code of a row of a DPM table.
  • col, col_init, col_end: A Reference to the code of a col of a DPM table.
  • sheet, sheet_init, sheet_end: A Reference to the code of a sheet of a DPM table.
  • interval_arithmetics: A Boolean value specifying whether interval arithmetics should apply. Only applicable to numeric types (Number, Integer). When true, numeric values are treated as intervals with centre equal to the value and radius calculated from the precision of the number. The default value, in case the parameter is omitted, is false.
  • default_value: A Scalar value specifying the value to be used in case of nulls. The value must be compatible with the Data Type of the selected Variable. The default value, in case the parameter is omitted, is null.
  • parameter: The code of a Parameter (back-door execution-time Scalar).
  • type: The declared Data Type of the Parameter. One of the scalar types number, integer, string, date, boolean, item, or the set types set-number, set-integer, set-string, set-date, set-boolean, set-item. See §3.1 Parameter Selection.

docs.title: 3.1.3 Output
docs.text:
rset<*> for Forms 1–4

scal<> for Form 5 with a scalar type (number, integer, string, date, boolean, item) — the Data Type is the one declared in the Parameter Selection*.

set<> for Form 5 with a set-* type (set-number, set-integer, set-string, set-date, set-boolean, set-item) — a set of values of the element type declared in the Parameter Selection*.

docs.title: 3.1.4 Semantics
docs.text: Serves to select data as defined in the DPM model. Parameter Selections (Form 5) additionally serve to inject Scalar values or sets of values supplied externally at execution time; see §3.1 Parameter Selection.

docs.title: 3.1.5 Additional Constraints
docs.text:
Constraints 1–5 apply to Forms 1–4. Constraint 6 applies to Form 5.

  1. Existence of the parameters. The referred table, Variable or Operation need to be defined in the DPM.
  2. Operations need to be defined in the same script.
  3. Rows, columns and sheets need to exist in the table or Operation on which they are defined.
  4. When the selection is done at Variable level, row, column and sheet parameters cannot exist.
  5. The interval parameter can only be set to true when the selected Variable has a numeric Data Type (Number or Integer).
  6. The declared type of a Parameter Selection must be one of the supported types and the optional default value must be compatible with that type:
    • Scalar types: number, integer, string, date, boolean, item. The default is a single literal (or an item reference for item).
    • Set types: set-number, set-integer, set-string, set-date, set-boolean, set-item. The default is a set literal whose elements are of the corresponding scalar type (e.g. default: {"AAA", "BBB"} for set-string, default: {[eba_CU:EUR]} for set-item).

docs.title: 3.1.6 Behaviour
docs.text:
Returns a Recordset with the following structure:

Key Components:

  • DPM-XL
  • Row: If the selected table has ordinate rows and more than one row is present in the selection. The name of the Component is "r".
  • Column: If the selected table has ordinate columns and more than one column is present in the selection. The name of the Component is "c".

  • Sheet: If the selected table has ordinate sheets and more than one sheet is present in the selection. The name of the Component is "s".

  • DPM-ML

  • X: If there is Row for DPM-XL.
  • Y: If there is Column for DPM-XL.

  • Z: If there is Sheet for DPM-XL.

  • A DPM Key Component for each Key Variable belonging to the Key associated to the selected Variable. The name of the Component is the Code of the Property associated to the Key Variable. The Data Type of the Component shall be the correspondent Data Type of the Metric or Property associated to the respective Key Variable.

Fact Component: With the Data Type corresponding to the selected Variable.

Attribute Components: One Component for each Attribute Variable associated to the selected Variable. The name of the Component is the Code of the Property associated to the Attribute Variable. The Data Type of the Component shall be the correspondent Data Type of the Metric or Property associated to the respective Attribute Variable.

On top of these, the contextual Components are latent in every selection, whether or not the selected Variables declare them: the Key Components refPeriod and entityID (§2.2.3.1.4) and the contextual Attribute Components (§2.2.3.3.1). They are added to the data structure of the Recordset only where an expression references them.

The Records for the Recordset shall be obtained from the input data according to the selection.

Ranges (e.g., r0010-0100) select all Headers whose codes fall between the start and end codes, inclusive on both boundaries. The ordering is lexicographic, based on the string representation of the Header codes. In the example, all Headers with a code lexicographically between 0010 and 0100 are selected.

When a table has a Header that is not open, the selection needs to have an explicit value for that Header. The wildcard * (e.g., r*, c*, s*) is used to select all Headers of the corresponding dimension.

When an Operation is selected (using the o prefix), the resulting Recordset has the same structure as the output of the referenced Operation. The Operation must be defined in the same script, either as a named Operation in the DPM or via a non-persistent assignment (:=). Row, column, and sheet parameters can be used to further refine the selection on the Operation result.

A Parameter Selection (Form 5, p prefix) returns a Scalar (for the basic types) or a set of values (for the set-* types) of the declared Data Type, rather than a Recordset. The value is supplied at execution time as part of the runtime input; when unbound, the Parameter takes the declared default, or null if no default is declared. See §3.1 Parameter Selection for the full specification.

docs.title: 3.1.6.1 Example: Using an Operation as Input
docs.text:
op1 := {tT1, r010-020, c010} * 10;
{tO1, r010, c010} <- {oOp1, r010} + {tT1, r010, c020}

In this example, op1 is assigned the result of multiplying the selection from table T1 by 10. The second statement selects row 010 from the result of op1 (using the o prefix) and adds it to a selection from table T1. The structure of {oOp1, r010} is determined by the output of op1, filtered by row 010.

docs.title: 3.1.7 DPM-ML Metamodel Representation
docs.text: There is no metamodel representation for the selection Operator. It is used to select, in last instance, Variables. So the result of the selection are processed to get the relevant Variables for DPM-ML, as well as the DefaultValue and UseIntervalArithmetics attributes.

docs.title: 3.2.1 Syntax
docs.text: with partial_selection [where_expression]1: expression

docs.title: 3.2.2 Input Parameters
docs.text:
• partial_selection: A selection expression (see Selection Operator)
  • expression: An expression including selection Operators
  • where_expression: An expression with a where operator

docs.title: 3.2.3 Output
docs.text: Does not generate output; modifies the selections of the expression after the colon.

docs.title: 3.2.4 Semantics
docs.text: Serves to simplify expressions by adding a single context that may apply to all the selection operators in the expression.

docs.title: 3.2.5 Additional Constraints
docs.text:
In case where_expression is used:

  • All the operands rising from selection operators have a where or a sub clause applicable, the one in the with, or the one overriding it. When the where_expression references Key Components, this implies that it is not possible to have a selection with a table that does not have open keys. A where_expression that only references the Fact Component (e.g. [where f != 0]) is applicable to any selection.

docs.title: 3.2.6 Behaviour
docs.text:
The selection parameters in the partial selection applies to all the selections in the expression, unless they are overridden by a more specific parameter.

Therefore, in a selection inside the expression, whenever one of the parameters of the selection expression is not present, but that parameter is present on the partial selection, the parameter of the partial selection applies.

In case where_expression is used, the overriding mechanism works as follows:

  • Any where clause used inside the expression fully overrides the where_expression, even if the properties used in the where clause inside the expression are different.
  • A sub clause used inside the expression fully overrides the where_expression.

docs.title: Example 1
docs.text:
with {tF_01.01, c0010, default: 0, interval: false}:
{r0010} = {r0020} + {r0030} + {r0040}

The partial selection applies to all the selections in the expression

docs.title: Example 2
docs.text:
with {tF_01.01, c0010, default: 0, interval: false}:
{r0010} + {r0040} = {tF_04.01, r0010, c0010}

The partial selection applies to the two selections that do not refer to a table. Regarding the other selection, the default and intervals apply

docs.title: Example 3
docs.text:
with {tF_01.01, c0010, default: 0, interval: false}:
{tF_01.01, r0010} + {tF_01.01, r0040} = {tF_04.01, r0010, c0010, default: null}

The partial selection applies to the two selections that refer to the same table referred to in the partial selection. Regarding the other selection, interval argument in the partial selection applies, but the default is overridden.

docs.title: Example 4
docs.text:
with {c0010, default: 0, interval: false}:
{tF_01.01, r0010} + {tF_01.01, r0040} = {tF_04.01, r0010}

The partial selection applies to all the selections in the expression.

docs.title: Example 5
docs.text:
with {tEXM, r0010}[where id1="ABC" and id2=5]:
  {c0010} = {c0020} + {c0030}

Where:

  • tEXM has two Key Components: id1 and id2

The clauses applying to each selection are:

Selection Clause {c0010} [where id1="ABC" and id2=5] {c0020} [where id1="ABC" and id2=5] {c0030} [where id1="ABC" and id2=5]

docs.text:
with {tEXM, r0010}[where id1="ABC" and id2=5]:

Where:

  • tEXM_02 has one Key Component: id1

The clauses applying to each selection are:

Selection Clause {c0010} [where id1="ABC" and id2=5] {c0020} [where id1="ABC" and id2=5] {tEXM_02, c0030} [where id1="ABC"]

docs.title: Example 7
docs.text:
with {r0010}[where id1="ABC"]:
  {tEXM, c0010} = {tEXM, c0020} + {tEXM_02, c0030}

Where:

  • tEXM has two Key Components: id1 and id2
  • tEXM_02 has one Key Component: id1

The clauses applying to each selection are:

Selection Clause {tEXM, c0010} [where id1="ABC"] {tEXM, c0020} [where id1="ABC"] {tEXM_02, c0030} [where id1="ABC"]

docs.title: Example 8
docs.text:
with {default: 0, interval: true}[where qEEA = [eba_qAE:qx2010]]:
if
    sum({tC_08.01.a, r0070, c0255}) 
       =
    sum({tC_08.01.a, r0010, c0255})
then
    sum
       ( filter ({tC_08.02, c0255}, {tC_08.02, c0010} = 1)) 
        =
    sum({tC_09.02, r0090, c0120} [where CEG = [eba_GA:qx2014]]) 
endif

Where:

  • C_08.01.a has one Key Component: qEEA
  • C_08.02 has two Key Components: qEEA and OGR
  • C_09.02 has oneKey Component: CEG

The clauses applying to each selection are:

Selection Clause {tC_08.01.a, r0070, c0255} [where qEEA = [eba_qAE:qx2010]] {tC_08.01.a, r0010, c0255} [where qEEA = [eba_qAE:qx2010]] {tC_08.02, c0255} [where qEEA = [eba_qAE:qx2010]] {tC_08.02, c0010} [where qEEA = [eba_qAE:qx2010]] {tC_09.02, r0090, c0120} [where CEG = [eba_GA:qx2014]]

docs.title: Example 9
docs.text:
with {tEXM, r0010}[where id1="ABC" and id2=5]:
  {c0010} = {c0020} + {tEXM_02, c0030}[sub id1="ABC"]

Where:

  • tEXM has two Key Components: id1 and id2
  • tEXM_02 has one Key Component: id1

The clauses applying to each selection are:

Selection Clause {c0010} [where id1="ABC" and id2=5] {c0020} [where id1="ABC" and id2=5] {tEXM_02, c0030} [sub id1="ABC"]

Note that the sub clause overrides the where in the with in the partial_selection.

docs.title: Example 10
docs.text:
with {tEXM, r0010}[where id1="ABC" and id2=5]:
  {c0010} = {c0020} + {tEXM_03, c0030}

Where:

  • tEXM has two Key Components: id1 and id2
  • tEXM_03 does not have any key component

This expression raises a Semantic Error, because the where clause applies to the operand {tEXM_03, c0030}, and this table doesnt have the referred Key Components.

docs.title: 4 Numeric Operators
docs.text: Numeric Operators describe operations involving Operands with data type Number, Integer or Number Interval.

docs.title: 4.1.1 Input Parameters
docs.text: Operands can be of Recordset or Scalar type. Must be defined as Number interval, Number, or Integer.

docs.title: 4.1.2 Result Type
docs.text: Recordset or Scalar with type Number interval, Number, or Integer.

docs.title: 4.1.3 Behaviour
docs.text:
If any Operand is null, then the result is also null.

Numeric Operators can be applied to any numeric type (Number interval, Number, or Integer) and combination of them, in which case casting to the highest type shall apply.

If the type of all Operands is Integer then the result has type Integer, unless the Operator's declared Output type does not include Integer (as is the case for division, exp, ln, log, sqrt, and power), in which case the result is implicitly promoted to Number (or Number Interval). For example, 7 / 2 returns 3.5, not 3. If any of the Operands is of type Number, and there are no Number intervals, then the result has type Number. If any Operand is of Number Interval type, the result has type Number Interval.

docs.title: 4.2.1.1 Syntax

docs.title: 4.2.1.2 Input Parameters

docs.title: 4.2.1.3 Output

docs.title: 4.2.1.4 Semantics

For intervals, returns the interval unchanged (both centre and radius are preserved).

docs.title: 4.2.1.6 Behaviour
docs.text:
• Unary Operators' standard behaviour.
  • Numeric Operators' standard behaviour.

docs.title: 4.2.1.7 Examples

  • + (-3) results in -3

docs.title: 4.3.2.5 Additional Constraints

docs.title: 4.3.3.1 Syntax
docs.text: left * right

docs.title: 4.3.3.2 Input Parameters
docs.text:
left: rset | scal <num + interval>

right: rset | scal <num + interval>

docs.title: 4.3.3.3 Output
docs.text: rset | scal <num + interval>

docs.title: 4.3.3.4 Semantics
docs.text:
Returns the product of two Numbers.

For intervals:

  • Centre is calculated as centre(left) * centre(right)
  • Radius is calculated as abs(centre(left) * radius(right)) + abs(radius(left) * centre(right)) + (radius(left) * radius(right))

docs.title: 4.3.3.5 Additional Constraints
docs.text: None.

docs.title: 4.3.3.6 Behaviour
docs.text:
• Binary Operators' standard behaviour
  • Numeric Operators' standard behaviour.

docs.title: 4.3.3.7 Examples
docs.text:
• 4 * 6 results in 24
  • -9 * 2 results in -18

docs.title: 4.3.4.1 Syntax
docs.text: num / den

docs.title: 4.3.4.2 Input Parameters
docs.text:
num: rset | scal <num + interval>

den: rset | scal <num + interval>

docs.title: 4.3.4.3 Output
docs.text: rset | scal <num + interval>

docs.title: 4.3.4.4 Semantics
docs.text:
Divides two Numbers.

For intervals: - Centre is calculated as centre(num) / centre(den) - Radius is calculated as:

max(
    abs(centre(num) + radius(num)) / (centre(den) + radius(den)),
    abs(centre(num) + radius(num)) / (centre(den) - radius(den)),
    abs(centre(num) - radius(num)) / (centre(den) + radius(den)),
    abs(centre(num) - radius(num)) / (centre(den) - radius(den))
) - abs(centre(num) / centre(den))

docs.title: 4.3.4.5 Additional Constraints
docs.text: The denominator interval must not contain zero, i.e., 0 must not be in the range [centre(den) - radius(den), centre(den) + radius(den)].

docs.title: 4.3.4.6 Behaviour
docs.text:
• Binary Operators' standard behaviour
  • Numeric Operators' standard behaviour.
  • If the denominator is 0, generates a run-time error.

docs.title: 4.3.4.7 Examples
docs.text:
• 24 / 6 results in 4
  • 7 / 2 results in 3.5
  • -18 / 2 results in -9

docs.title: 4.3.5.1 Syntax

docs.title: 4.3.5.2 Input Parameters

docs.title: 4.3.5.3 Output

docs.title: 4.3.5.4 Semantics
docs.text:

For intervals:

  • Centre is the maximum of the centres of all the Operands.
  • Radius is the radius of the Operand with the maximum centre. If multiple Operands share the same maximum centre, the largest radius among them is taken.

docs.title: 4.3.5.5 Additional Constraints
docs.text: None.

docs.title: 4.3.5.6 Behaviour
docs.text: • For each pair of Operands, the standard behaviour for binary Operators applies.

docs.title: 4.3.5.7 Examples
docs.text:
• max(1, 3, -5) results in 3
  • max(1, 3, null) results in null

docs.title: 5.1 Comparison Operators' General Behaviour
docs.text:
Comparison Operators describe operations that compare the values of Operands.

This Operator group is based upon the General behavior for binary Operators.

docs.title: 5.1.1 Input Parameters
docs.text: Operands that can be of Recordset or Scalar type. Must have the same Data Type. For all Operators that accept numeric Operands, intervals are allowed.

docs.title: 5.1.2 Result Type
docs.text: Recordset or Scalar with type Boolean.

docs.title: 5.1.3 Constraints
docs.text: The Operands for the comparison operations must be of the same type (considering implicit casting).

docs.title: 5.1.4 Behaviour
docs.text:
If any Operand is null, then the result is also null.

For comparison Operators implying an order (>, >=, <, <=), the following rules apply:

  • Boolean values: true is considered greater than false.
  • Strings: Alphabetic order is followed.

docs.title: 5.2.1.1 Syntax
docs.text: left = right

docs.title: 5.2.1.2 Input Parameters
docs.text:
left: rset | scal | scalar_set <*>

right: rset | scal | scalar_set <*>

docs.title: 5.2.1.3 Output
docs.text: rset | scal <boo>

docs.title: 5.2.1.4 Semantics
docs.text:
Returns true if left is equal to right and false otherwise.

For intervals: abs(centre(left) – centre(right)) <= radius(left) + radius(right).

When both Operands are set-valued (a set literal, a Subcategory, a set-* Parameter, or the result of a set Operator), = denotes set equality: it compares them as Scalar Sets and returns a single Boolean — see Set Equality.

docs.title: 5.2.1.5 Additional Constraints
docs.text: • A Scalar Set Operand may only be compared with another Scalar Set: both left and right must be set-valued. Comparing a Scalar Set with a Scalar or Recordset is not allowed.

docs.title: 5.2.1.6 Behaviour
docs.text:
• Binary Operators' standard behaviour.
  • Comparison Operators' standard behaviour.

docs.title: 5.2.1.7 Examples
docs.text:
• 1 = 2 results in false
  • 3 = null results in null
  • "4" = "4" results in true

docs.text: left != right

docs.title: 5.3.1.2 Input Parameters

docs.title: 5.3.1.5 Additional Constraints

docs.title: 5.3.1.6 Behaviour
docs.text:
• Binary Operators' standard behaviour.
  • Comparison Operators' standard behaviour.

docs.title: 5.3.1.7 Examples

  • "4" != "4" results in false

docs.title: 5.8.1.1 Syntax
docs.text: op in set

docs.title: 5.8.1.2 Input Parameters
docs.text:
op: rset | scal <*>

set: scalar_set <*> | subcategory

The set Operand may be any set-valued expression: a set literal ({v1, v2, ...}), a Subcategory, a Parameter of a set-* type, or the result of a Set Operator — set_of, union, intersect, setdiff or symdiff (see Set Operators).

docs.title: 5.8.1.3 Output
docs.text: rset | scal <boo>

docs.title: 5.8.1.4 Semantics
docs.text:
Returns true if op belongs to the set and false otherwise.

op in {v1, v2, ...} is semantically equivalent to op = v1 or op = v2 or .... Therefore, for intervals, this operator follows the interval semantics of the equality operator (=): the result is true if the interval overlaps (in the sense of =) with at least one element of the set.

Since set elements are typically points, and the point-to-interval promotion rule (§2.2.4) converts each point v to an interval with centre v and radius 0, this reduces to:

abs(centre(op) – v) <= radius(op)

for each element v in the set. The overall result is true if this condition holds for any element.
