docs.title: 7.1 Aggregate Operators' General Behaviour
docs.text:
Aggregate Operators apply a summarising computation (sum, count, average, …) to the Fact values of the Operand Recordset. They support two mutually exclusive invocation styles:

  • A reducing invocation — the group by clause, or no clause at all — which collapses each group of Records into a single result Record: N Records per group become one. This is the classic aggregation and is the subject of §7.1.1–§7.1.7.
  • An analytical invocation — the over clause — which computes the same aggregate over a window of related Records but returns one output Record per input Record, so the Recordset keeps its cardinality. Analytical invocations are the unifying mechanism behind moving averages, running totals, shares of a parent total and ranks. They are described in §7.1.8.

The group by and over clauses are mutually exclusive: an invocation uses either group by (or nothing) or over, never both.

docs.title: 7.1.1 Syntax
docs.text:
aggregateOperator ( op {group by groupingId {, groupingId}*} )

aggregateOperator ( op over ( analyticClause ) )

docs.title: 7.1.2 Input Parameters
docs.text:
op: rset <*>

groupingId: scal <prop>

docs.title: 7.1.3 Output
docs.text: rset | scal <*>

docs.title: 7.1.4 Semantics
docs.text:
In the reducing invocation, aggregate Operators perform operations on the measures of the Operand Recordset, calculating the required aggregated values for groups of Records. The groups of Records to be aggregated are specified through the grouping clause. If no grouping clause is used, the operation shall be calculated on all the Records, resulting in a Scalar.

In the analytical invocation, the same computation is applied without reducing: for each input Record the Operator is evaluated over the window of Records defined by the over clause, and the result replaces that Record's Fact value. The output has the same Key Components and the same number of Records as the input (see §7.1.8).

docs.title: 7.1.5 Additional Constraints
docs.text:
The allowed Data Types depend on the specific Operator according to the following table:

Operator Operand Type Result Type Sum Number Number Count Any Integer Min Any Any Max Any Any Average Number Number Median Number Number Rank Any Integer

For Average and Median, when all input values are Integer, the result is implicitly promoted to Number — the result type is always Number, even on integer-only inputs (e.g., avg(1, 2) returns 1.5; median(1, 2, 3, 4) returns 2.5). For Sum, an Integer-only input yields an Integer result. Count always returns Integer by definition. Min and Max return one of the input values, so an Integer-only input yields an Integer result. Rank (§7.8) exists only in the analytical invocation and always returns Integer.

The Components named in the grouping clause, and in the partition by and order by sub-clauses of the over clause, shall be present in the Operand.

docs.title: 7.1.6 Behaviour
docs.text:
In the reducing invocation, aggregate Operations generate a Recordset or a Scalar, depending on the grouping clause.

If the grouping clause exists, the structure of the resulting Recordset has as Key Components the Components in the group by

The result may be:

  • A Recordset, for which the resulting structure contains as Key dimensions the Components included in the group by clause.
  • A Scalar, if the grouping clause is omitted.

In the analytical invocation (over clause), the result is always a Recordset with the same Key Components and the same number of Records as the Operand (see §7.1.8).

Null values are excluded from the calculations. If all input values (in a group, or in a Record's window) are null, the result is null. The only exception is Count, which returns 0 in that case (see below).

docs.title: 7.1.6.1 Empty Operands
docs.text:
An aggregation has no values to work with when its Operand contains no Records, or when every one of its input values has been excluded as null. In that case:

  • Count returns 0. Counting is a question about the collection rather than about the values, and the empty collection has a well-defined answer. Count therefore never returns null: its result is always a non-negative Integer.
  • Sum, Min, Max, Average and Median return null. These Operators are defined over the input values, and with no values there is no result to report.

In particular, Sum over an empty Operand is null and not 0. Although 0 is the identity element of addition, returning it would state that a total of zero was reported, when in fact nothing was reported at all. This also keeps the empty case consistent with the all-null case: since null values are excluded before the calculation, an all-null Operand is an empty Operand, and both yield null.

When a grouping clause is present, the exclusion of null values takes place within each group and not before the grouping. The groups are derived from the Records present in the Operand, and a Record whose value is null still determines a group. A group all of whose values are null therefore does exist, and the rules above apply to it: Count returns 0 for that group and the other Operators return null for it. Retaining the group preserves the information that the Records were there, so that the nvl Operator or any subsequent Operation can act on the result.

What cannot happen is a group emerging for a Key combination that is not present in the Operand. The values of the Key Components of a group have to be taken from a Record, and Key Components cannot be empty, so no Record can be produced for a combination that was never reported: DPM-XL does not build the Cartesian product of all the potential combinations of Key values (see Implicit Nulls Generation, where implicit nulls are generated only for the Key combinations having at least one value reported). Accordingly, an Operand with no Records at all yields an empty Recordset, and not a Recordset holding a Record with the value 0 or null.

Whether a null is explicit or implicit makes no difference to any of the above, in line with Implicit and Explicit Null Values. What determines the result is whether a Record exists in the Operand, not the reason why its value is null.

docs.title: 7.1.7 Examples
docs.text:
Supposing the following Recordset with name rs1:

r c CNT f 010 010 PT 100 010 020 PT 200 020 010 PT 300 020 020 PT 400 010 010 DE 500 010 020 DE 600 020 010 DE 700 020 020 DE 800

sum(rs1 group by r) results in:

r f 010 1400 020 2200

sum(rs1 group by r, CNT) results in:

r CNT f 010 PT 300 020 PT 700 010 DE 1100 020 DE 1500

count(rs1) results in: 8 (Scalar)

Supposing now a Recordset with name rs2 whose selection yields no Records at all:

  • count(rs2) results in: 0 (Scalar)
  • sum(rs2) results in: null (Scalar)
  • sum(rs2 group by r) results in an empty Recordset with Key Component r and no Records.
  • count(rs2 group by r) results in the same empty Recordset, and not in a Record holding the value 0. Under a grouping clause there is no Record to provide a value for r, so the 0 has nowhere to appear. Count and Sum thus give the same result here, and only differ in the Scalar case above.

Supposing instead a Recordset with name rs3 having the same Records as rs1, but with all the values of f null:

  • count(rs3) results in: 0 (Scalar)
  • sum(rs3) results in: null (Scalar)
  • sum(rs3 group by r) results in:
r f 010 null 020 null
  • count(rs3 group by r) results in:
r f 010 0 020 0

The groups for r are still formed, because the Records are present in rs3 and provide the values of r. This is the only way a Count of 0 can appear in a grouped result.

docs.title: 7.1.8 The Analytical Invocation (over clause)
docs.text: The over clause turns an aggregate Operator into an analytical invocation (a window function in SQL terms). Instead of collapsing groups, the Operator computes its result over a window of Records defined relative to each Record, and emits one output Record per input Record.

docs.title: 7.1.8.1 Syntax
docs.text:
op over ( {partition by partitionId {, partitionId}*} {order by orderId {asc|desc} {, orderId {asc|desc}}*} {windowClause} )

where

windowClause: ( data points | range ) between windowBoundary and windowBoundary

windowBoundary: unbounded preceding | unbounded following | current data point | int {time_period_code} preceding | int {time_period_code} following

partitionId, orderId: scal <prop>

int: A positive Integer literal.

time_period_code: One of the time-period codes A, S, Q, M, W, D.

All three inner sub-clauses are optional, subject to the constraints below. asc (ascending) is the default direction and may be omitted.

docs.title: 7.1.8.2 Partitioning (partition by)
docs.text:
partition by splits the Operand Recordset into groups (partitions) that share the same values for the listed Components, analogously to the Key Components of a reducing group by. Every Record's window is confined to its own partition. When partition by is omitted, the whole Recordset is a single partition.

Unlike group by, partition by does not reduce: the partition Components are not the Key of the result — the result keeps the Key Components of the Operand.

docs.title: 7.1.8.3 Ordering (order by)
docs.text:
Records are an unordered collection (see §2.2.3), so any order-dependent window needs an explicit ordering. order by establishes, within each partition, the order in which Records are considered. Each ordering Component may be followed by asc (ascending, the default) or desc (descending).

order by is:

  • required for order-dependent Operators (rank) and whenever a data points or range window clause is used;
  • optional otherwise — when omitted the whole partition forms one unordered window and every Record in the partition receives the same aggregate.

These requirements are stated as constraints in §7.1.8.6.

docs.title: 7.1.8.4 Window Clause (data points / range)
docs.text:
The window clause narrows the window to a band of Records around the current one, expressed as two bounds. A window clause requires an order by.

Each bound is a windowBoundary, written in the direction it travels from the current Record:

  • current data point — the current Record itself.
  • n preceding / n following — n units before or after the current Record, where n is a positive Integer. The zero offset is written current data point.
  • unbounded preceding / unbounded following — the start or the end of the partition.

The unit of n depends on the keyword introducing the clause:

  • data points counts positional offsets: n is a number of Records in the order by order, so 1 preceding is the immediately preceding Record. Use data points when position — not the value of the order key — is what matters.
  • range counts value offsets on a single order by Component: the window contains every Record whose order value lies within n of the current Record's order value. Use range when the ordering has gaps, because the window is defined by the order value rather than by record position.

Where the order by Component is of Date type, n is followed by a time-period code giving the unit of the offset, so that 11 M preceding is the Record eleven months before the current one. The offset is computed exactly as in time_shift: n units of the given period are subtracted from (preceding) or added to (following) the current Record's order value, and the bound is that resulting date. Where the order by Component is numeric, n is a plain number of units of that Component and no period code is written.

preceding and following are always relative to the order by order, not to the natural order of the values: a preceding bound lies toward the start of the ordering and a following bound toward its end. Under a desc ordering the start of the ordering holds the greatest order values, so a preceding bound then has a greater order value than the current Record — a later date, where the order key is a Date. This is the same rule data points follows, where 1 preceding is the previous Record of the ordering whichever direction it runs.

A trailing window therefore requires an ascending ordering. order by refDate range between 11 M preceding and current data point covers the twelve months ending at the current Record, whereas the same window clause under order by refDate desc reaches forward instead, over the twelve months beginning at it.

When the window clause is omitted, the window is the whole partition (still honouring order by where it matters, as for rank). A time-period code may be written only on a range bound whose order by Component is of Date type; it is not allowed on a data points bound, whose unit is always one Record. The bounds are further constrained as set out in §7.1.8.6.

docs.title: 7.1.8.5 Structure and Records
docs.text: The result is a Recordset with the same Key Components and the same number of Records as the Operand. Each Record's Fact value is replaced by the aggregate computed over that Record's window; Key Components are unchanged and Attribute Components are not propagated. Null values inside a window are excluded from the computation, consistent with the reducing invocation; if a window contains only nulls, the result for that Record follows the empty-Operand rules of §7.1.6.1 — 0 for Count, null for the other Operators. The result Data Type of each Operator is the one given in §7.1.5.

docs.title: 7.1.8.6 Additional Constraints
docs.text:
The Components named in partition by and in order by shall be present in the Operand, as required by §7.1.5.

The offset n. The n of n preceding or n following shall be at least 1. The zero offset — the current Record itself — is written current data point, which is its only form: 0 preceding, 0 following and 0 M preceding are not allowed.

When an order by is required. order by is required in two cases: when a window clause is used, and always with the rankoperator. Both narrow or read a sequence, and Records are an unordered collection (§2.2.3), so without an explicit ordering neither has a determined result. This holds even for between unbounded preceding and unbounded following, whose meaning does not in fact depend on the ordering: the whole partition is expressed by omitting the window clause, which is the form to use.

rank takes no window clause. rank ranks by the order by value, and a window clause is defined along that same order by, positionally for data points and by value for range. A frame can therefore never give rank a different comparison group to measure against. To compare a Record against a window of its neighbours, use an aggregate over that window and compare it with the Record's own value, as in max_aggr(rs1 over (partition by qInstrument order by refDate range between 11 M preceding and current data point)).

The order by of a range clause. Where the window clause is a range, the order by shall name exactly one Component, and that Component shall be of Date, Number or Integer type. A range bound measures an offset against the order value, and a lexicographic ordering over several Components offers no single value to offset from, while a String or Boolean Component offers no notion of lying within n of a value. Neither restriction applies to data points, which needs only a sequence, nor to rank; both accept several ordering Components.

Ordering of the window bounds. The bounds of a window clause are ordered by the position they denote relative to the current Record:

unbounded preceding < n preceding (decreasing in n) < current data point < n following (increasing in n) < unbounded following

  • The first bound shall not be after the second in this order. Where the two bounds denote the same position, the window is that single position — as in between current data point and current data point.
  • unbounded following shall not be the first bound, and unbounded preceding shall not be the second. Such a window is either empty or a single Record of the partition repeated for every Record, which is never the intent: the whole partition is written between unbounded preceding and unbounded following, and a single aggregate over the partition is a reducing invocation (§7.1.6).

Commensurable period codes. Where both bounds of a range clause carry a time-period code, the two codes shall be commensurable: either both drawn from A, S, Q, M, or both from W, D. Within each of these groups every code is a whole number of the same base unit (twelve, six, three and one months; seven and one days), so the bounds can always be ordered. Across the groups they cannot: 1 M preceding is earlier than 30 D preceding in some months and later in others, so a frame such as range between 3 M preceding and 40 D preceding has no determinate meaning and is not allowed.

docs.title: 7.1.8.7 Examples
docs.text:
Considering the following Recordset with name rs1, holding a monthly balance per instrument:

qInstrument refDate f A 2022-01-01 100 A 2022-02-01 200 A 2022-03-01 300 B 2022-01-01 10 B 2022-02-01 20 B 2022-03-01 30

Trailing 2-month moving average — avg(rs1 over (partition by qInstrument order by refDate data points between 1 preceding and current data point)) averages each Record with the immediately preceding one in its partition:

qInstrument refDate f A 2022-01-01 100 A 2022-02-01 150 A 2022-03-01 250 B 2022-01-01 10 B 2022-02-01 15 B 2022-03-01 25

(The first Record of each partition has no predecessor, so its window is just itself.)

Running total — sum(rs1 over (partition by qInstrument order by refDate data points between unbounded preceding and current data point)) accumulates from the start of each partition up to the current Record:

qInstrument refDate f A 2022-01-01 100 A 2022-02-01 300 A 2022-03-01 600 B 2022-01-01 10 B 2022-02-01 30 B 2022-03-01 60

12-month moving average, gap-tolerant — avg(rs1 over (partition by qInstrument order by refDate range between 11 M preceding and current data point)) averages every Record whose refDate falls within the 12 calendar months ending at the current Record. Because the bound is value-based, a missing month simply contributes no Record to the window; the positional form data points between 11 preceding and current data point would instead always reach 11 Records back, ignoring calendar gaps.

docs.title: 7.3.1 Syntax

docs.title: 7.3.2 Input Parameters

docs.title: 7.3.3 Output

docs.title: 7.3.4 Semantics
docs.text:
Returns the number of non-null values in the Recordset or in each group of Records. Follows the general semantics of aggregate Operators: null values are excluded from the calculation, so Records whose value is null do not contribute to the count.

Unlike the other aggregate Operators, count never returns null. Its result is always a non-negative Integer: an Operand with no Records, and an Operand whose values are all null, both yield 0 (see Empty Operands).

When op is a scalar_set, count returns the cardinality of the set — the number of distinct elements it contains. As sets are duplicate-free and never contain null (see Set Operators' general behaviour), the count is taken over the distinct, non-null values. The group by clause is inapplicable when op is a scalar_set.

docs.title: 7.3.5 Additional Constraints
docs.text: None.

docs.title: 7.3.6 Behaviour
docs.text:
Aggregate Operators' general behaviour.

Note: Aggregate Operators generally ignore null values. This behavior can be overridden by using the nvl Operator. Applied to count, count(nvl(op, 0)) counts every Record of op, including those whose value is null.

docs.text:

  • count(set_of({tT1, r010-020}[get CNT])) results in 4 — the number of distinct CNT values (see set_of).
  • count(union({1, 2}, {2, 3})) results in 3.
  • count({}) results in 0 — the cardinality of the empty set.

docs.title: 7.8 Rank (rank)

docs.title: 7.8.1 Syntax

docs.title: 7.8.4 Semantics
docs.text:

Records that tie on the order value receive the same rank, and the next distinct value's rank is increased by the number of tied Records (standard competition ranking: 1, 2, 2, 4, …).

rank is order-dependent, so the over clause must contain an order by, and it takes no window clause: rank always considers the whole partition. The reason is that the order by is both the ranking key and the axis along which a window clause would be defined, so a frame could only report the Record's position inside the frame rather than its standing within a comparison group (see §7.1.8.6).

Records whose order value is null sort last and share the final rank group.

docs.title: 7.8.5 Additional Constraints
docs.text:
• The over clause must contain an order by.
  • partition by is optional; without it the whole Recordset is ranked as a single partition.
  • A window clause (data points / range) is not allowed with rank.

docs.title: 7.8.6 Behaviour
docs.text: Aggregate Operators' analytical invocation behaviour: one output Record per input Record, with the Fact Component replaced by the Integer rank. Key Components are unchanged and Attribute Components are not propagated.

docs.title: 7.8.7 Examples
docs.text:
Considering the following Recordset with name rs1, holding total assets per entity within each country:

qCountry id f PT X 300 PT Y 100 PT Z 300 DE P 500 DE Q 200

Rank within country by total assets (descending) — rank(rs1 over (partition by qCountry order by f desc)) returns:

qCountry id f PT X 1 PT Z 1 PT Y 3 DE P 1 DE Q 2

(Within PT, the two Records valued 300 tie at rank 1, so the 100 Record takes rank 3. The Fact value is replaced by the rank.)

docs.title: 8.1.1 Syntax
docs.text: if conditionExpression then thenExpression {else elseExpression} endif

docs.title: 8.1.2 Input Parameters
docs.text:
conditionExpression: rset | scal <boo>

thenExpression: rset | scal <*>

elseExpression: rset | scal <*>

docs.title: 8.1.3 Output
docs.text: rset | scal <*>

docs.title: 8.1.4 Semantics
docs.text: The result combines values selected from the thenExpression where the conditionExpression evaluates to true, with values selected from the elseExpression where the conditionExpression evaluates to false or null. Records are matched between the conditionExpression and each branch by inner join. When the elseExpression is omitted, Records where the conditionExpression is not true are excluded from the result. The formal evaluation is given in §8.1.6.

docs.title: 8.1.5 Additional Constraints
docs.text:
The additional constraints ensure that the structure of the output is known at compile time and that no Record in the result can have a null value in any Key Component.

To the effects of these additional constraints, Scalars are treated as Recordsets with zero Key Components.

  • Data Type compatibility: The thenExpression and elseExpression (when provided) must be of the same Data Type, or of Data Types that admit implicit casting per the casting rules in §2.3.2. When implicit casting applies, the resulting Data Type is that common Data Type.
  • Structure compatibility with the condition: The Key Components of the thenExpression must be compatible with those of the conditionExpression — that is, one set must be equal to, or a subset of, the other, following the same rule as for binary Operators on two Recordsets. If the elseExpression is provided, the same restriction applies to the elseExpression together with the conditionExpression.
  • Matched join structure: When the elseExpression is provided, the Key Components of the thenExpression and the elseExpression must satisfy one of: a) they are the same; or b) both are equal to, or a subset of, those of the conditionExpression.
  • Null literal exception: When thenExpression or elseExpression is null (explicit or, in the case of elseExpression, implicit because not used), it is possible for the other expression to have a set of key components that is a superset of the conditionExpression. This is allowed because null records are not added to the output, and therefore no records with null value for Key components may arise.

docs.title: 8.1.6 Behaviour
docs.text:
Throughout this section, join(x, y) denotes the inner join of §2.2.3.3; its result is a Recordset whose Key Components are the superset of those of x and y (which, under the Structure compatibility with the condition constraint, equals the Key Components of whichever operand is the superset). This makes the Matched join structure constraint of §8.1.5 equivalent to requiring that join(conditionExpression, thenExpression) and join(conditionExpression, elseExpression) have the same structure: case (a) gives both joins the Key Components conditionExpression ∪ thenExpression = conditionExpression ∪ elseExpression; case (b) gives both joins the Key Components of the conditionExpression.

  • Structure:
    • If all operands are Scalars (zero Key Components), the result is a Scalar; otherwise the result is a Recordset.
    • The structure of the output shall contain the largest set of Key Components of the input structures.
  • Evaluation:
    • The expression is evaluated as the disjoint union of two sets of Records:
      • The Records of join(conditionExpression, thenExpression) for which the conditionExpression evaluates to true, with the value of the Fact Component taken from the thenExpression.
      • When the elseExpression is provided: the Records of join(conditionExpression, elseExpression) for which the conditionExpression evaluates to false or null, with the value taken from the elseExpression.
    • The two sets are disjoint by construction (they select complementary Records of the conditionExpression) and share the same structure by the Matched join structure constraint.
  • Omitted else: Records where the conditionExpression evaluates to false or null are not included in the result.

The following table summarises the allowed combinations, the additional constraint that applies beyond pairwise structure compatibility, and the resulting structure:

To the effects of this table:

  • An explicit else null is treated as a missing else.
  • When thenExpression or elseExpression is the literal null, the Null literal exception of §8.1.5 may further relax the constraints in the corresponding row, since no Records are contributed by a null branch.
Condition Then Else Additional constraint Result structure Scalar Scalar — — Scalar Scalar Scalar Scalar — Scalar Scalar Recordset — — Recordset (keys of then) Scalar Recordset Recordset then and else must have the same Key Components Recordset (common keys of then and else) Scalar Scalar Recordset Forbidden — join structures differ — Scalar Recordset Scalar Forbidden — join structures differ — Recordset Scalar — — Recordset (keys of condition) Recordset Scalar Scalar — Recordset (keys of condition) Recordset Scalar Recordset Key Components of else ⊆ those of condition Recordset (keys of condition) Recordset Recordset — Key Components of then and condition: equal or one a subset of the other Recordset (superset of keys) Recordset Recordset Scalar Key Components of then ⊆ those of condition Recordset (keys of condition) Recordset Recordset Recordset join(condition, then) and join(condition, else) must share the same structure Recordset (common join structure)

Relation to other operators: Under this definition, if-then-else subsumes several other operators as equivalent idioms:

  • if A then B (no else), when the Key Components of A are a subset of those of B, is equivalent to filter(B, A).
  • if isnull(A) then B else A is equivalent to nvl(A, B) when A and B share the same data structure (the case in which nvl is applicable).
  • if A = x then y else A is a general pattern to replace a value x with y.

docs.title: Example 1: Scalar condition, scalar branches
docs.text:
if 10 > 5 then 100 else 200 endif

Result: 100 (scalar). The condition is true, so the then branch is returned.

docs.title: Example 2: Scalar condition, recordset branches
docs.text:
Supposing {tT1, r010-020} yields:

r f 010 100 020 200

And {tT2, r010-020} yields:

r f 010 900 020 800 
if 10 > 5 then {tT1, r010-020} else {tT2, r010-020} endif

Result:

r f 010 100 020 200

The condition is true, so the entire then recordset is returned.

docs.title: Example 3: Recordset condition, scalar branches
docs.text:
Supposing {tT1, r010-020} > 150 yields:

r f 010 false 020 true 
if {tT1, r010-020} > 150 then 1 else 0 endif

Result:

r f 010 0 020 1

The condition is evaluated per record. The scalar branches are applied to each record based on its condition value.

docs.title: Example 4: Recordset condition, recordset branches with same keys
docs.text:
Supposing {tT1, r010-020} yields:

r f 010 100 020 200

And {tT2, r010-020} yields:

r f 010 900 020 800 
if {tT1, r010-020} > 150 then {tT1, r010-020} else {tT2, r010-020} endif

Result:

r f 010 900 020 200

Record 010 takes the else value (100 is not > 150), record 020 takes the then value (200 > 150).

docs.title: Example 5: Forbidden — scalar condition with mixed branches
docs.text:
The following expression is not allowed:

if {tT1, r010} > 150 then {tT2, r010-020} else 0 endif

The condition {tT1, r010} > 150 is a Scalar Boolean. The then branch is a Recordset with Key Components {r} and the else branch is a Scalar (zero Key Components). Applying the Matched join structure constraint: join(condition, then) has keys {r} while join(condition, else) has no keys. Since these structures differ, the expression is rejected. To fix this, either omit the else branch (records where the condition is false or null will not appear in the result) or replace the else branch with a Recordset sharing the same Key Components as the then branch.

docs.title: Example 6: Recordset condition with more keys than the branches
docs.text:
Supposing {tT1, r010-020} is an open table with a Key Component CNT, and the condition {tT1, r010-020} > 0 yields:

r CNT f 010 ES true 010 PT false 020 ES true 020 PT true

And the then branch {tT2, r010-020} has only the r key:

r f 010 100 020 200 
if {tT1, r010-020} > 0 then {tT2, r010-020} else 0 endif

The condition has keys {r, CNT} and the then branch has keys {r}. The result has the structure of the superset (the condition), and the then/else values are matched via inner join on the common key (r):

r CNT f 010 ES 100 010 PT 0 020 ES 200 020 PT 200

docs.title: Example 7: Omitted else
docs.text:
Supposing {tT1, r010-020} yields:

r f 010 100 020 200 
if {tT1, r010-020} > 150 then {tT1, r010-020} endif

Result:

r f 020 200

Record 010 is excluded because its condition value is false (100 is not > 150). Record 020 is included with its then value.

docs.title: Example 8: Forbidden — branches with incompatible key structures
docs.text:
Supposing {tT1, r010-020} has Key Component r and yields:

r f 010 200 020 100

And {tT3, r010-020} has Key Components r and CNT and yields:

r CNT f 020 ES 500 020 PT 600

The following expression is not allowed:

if {tT1, r010-020} > 150 then 0 else {tT3, r020} endif

join(condition, then) has keys {r} while join(condition, else) has keys {r, CNT}. Since the structures differ, the Matched join structure constraint rejects the expression at compile time. This prevents results where records of the condition would silently disappear because one branch cannot supply values for the key tuples required by the other (while the same records would be included if the elseExpression was omitted). To fix this, ensure both branches produce results with the same Key Components after joining with the condition.

docs.title: Example 9: Null literal exception — then branch with more keys than the condition
docs.text:
Supposing the condition {tT1, r010-020} > 0 yields a Recordset with key {r}:

r f 010 true 020 false

And the then branch {tT2, r010-020} is an open table with keys {r, CNT}:

r CNT f 010 ES 100 010 PT 200 020 ES 300 020 PT 400 
if {tT1, r010-020} > 0 then {tT2, r010-020} endif

With no else clause, the elseExpression is implicitly the literal null. The Matched join structure constraint would normally reject this — join(condition, then) has Key Components {r, CNT} while join(condition, null) has {r} — but the Null literal exception of §8.1.5 admits the case because the implicit-null branch contributes no Records, so no Record with a null value in a Key Component can arise.

Result:

r CNT f 010 ES 100 010 PT 200

The result takes the structure of the then branch, {r, CNT}. Records (010, ES) and (010, PT) are included (the condition is true for r = 010); Records with r = 020 are excluded because the condition is false and the implicit-null else branch contributes nothing.

docs.title: 8.2.1 Syntax
docs.text: nvl( op1, op2 )

docs.title: 8.2.2 Input Parameters
docs.text:
op1: rset | scal <*>

op2: rset | scal <*>

docs.title: 8.2.3 Output
docs.text: rset | scal <*>

docs.title: 8.2.4 Semantics
docs.text: Returns op2 when op1 is null, otherwise op1.

docs.title: 8.2.5 Additional Constraints
docs.text:
op1 and op2 need to be of the same type (Scalar or Recordset) and same Data Type.

If op1 and op2 are of the Recordset type, they need to have the same data structure.

docs.title: 8.2.6 Behaviour
docs.text: Binary Operators' standard behaviour.

docs.title: 8.2.7 Examples
docs.text:
Scalar example

nvl({tT1, r010, c010, s01}, 0) returns 0 when the selected cell is null, otherwise returns the cell value.

Recordset example

Considering the following Recordset from {tT1, r010}:

CNT f ES 100 PT null DE null IT 400

And the substitution Recordset (same structure, all zeros):

CNT f ES 0 PT 0 DE 0 IT 0

nvl({tT1, r010}, {tT1_default, r010}) returns:

CNT f ES 100 PT 0 DE 0 IT 400

Records where op1 is not null are kept as-is; Records where op1 is null take the value from op2.

docs.title: 8.3.1 Syntax
docs.text: filter( filteredOp, filteringOp )

docs.title: 8.3.2 Input Parameters
docs.text:
filteredOp: rset <*>

filteringOp: rset <boo>

docs.title: 8.3.3 Output
docs.text: rset <*>

docs.title: 8.3.4 Semantics
docs.text: Returns the Records of the filteredOp Recordset for which their matching Record in filteringOp evaluates to true. Records whose matching value in filteringOp is false or null are excluded (per the null-as-false rule for filtering in §4.3).

docs.title: 8.3.5 Additional Constraints
docs.text: filteringOp must have the same Key Components as filteredOp or a subset of them.

docs.title: 8.3.6 Behaviour
docs.text:
Returns a Recordset with the same data structure as filteredOp.

An inner join between filteredOp and filteringOp is performed. The Records in filteredOp that match to a Record in filteringOp with true value are returned.

docs.title: 8.3.7 Examples
docs.text:
Considering the following Recordset from {tT1, r010}:

CNT f ES 100 PT 200 DE 300 IT 400

filter({tT1, r010}, {tT1, r010} > 150) keeps only the Records whose fact value is greater than 150:

CNT f PT 200 DE 300 IT 400

The filtering Operand {tT1, r010} > 150 evaluates to a Boolean Recordset with the same Key Components. Only the Records where the Boolean value is true are retained; false and null values cause the corresponding Record to be excluded.

docs.title: 9.3.1 Syntax
docs.text: substr( op, {start}, {length} )

docs.title: 9.3.2 Input Parameters
docs.text:
op: rset | scal <str>

start: scal <int>

length: scal <int>

docs.title: 9.3.3 Output
docs.text: rset | scal <str>

docs.title: 9.3.4 Semantics
docs.text:
Extracts the substring of op that begins at the character in position start (the first character of op is in position 1) and runs for length characters.

start and length are optional. If start is omitted, extraction begins at the first character of op. If length is omitted, the substring runs to the end of op. If both are omitted, the whole op string is returned.

docs.title: 9.3.5 Additional Constraints
docs.text:
• start must be greater than or equal to 1.
  • length must be greater than or equal to 0. A length of 0 is permitted (and returns an empty string) so that a length derived from another expression, such as the difference between two positions, can collapse to an empty span without raising an error.

docs.title: 9.3.6 Behaviour
docs.text:
• Unary Operators' standard behaviour.
  • If start is greater than the number of characters of op, an empty string is returned.
  • If start + length goes past the end of op, the substring ends at the last character of op.

docs.title: 9.3.7 Examples
docs.text:
• substr("Hello World", 7) results in "World"
  • substr("Hello World", 1, 5) results in "Hello"
  • substr("Hello World", 7, 100) results in "World"
  • substr("Hello World") results in "Hello World"
  • substr("Hello World", 20) results in ""
  • substr("Hello World", 7, 0) results in "" (a length of 0 extracts no characters)
  • substr(null, 2, 3) results in null

docs.title: 10.2 Date-component Extraction
docs.text: The Operators in this section extract a single calendar component (year, semester, quarter, month, week or day) from a Date. They all share the same syntax, input/output types and null-propagation behaviour; they differ only in the component returned and in how they handle Date notations that do not pin down the requested component.

docs.title: 10.2.1.1 Syntax
docs.text:
\<op>( op )

where <op> is one of year, semester, quarter, month, week, day.

docs.title: 10.2.1.2 Input Parameters

docs.title: 10.2.1.3 Output
docs.text:
rset <int> | scal <int>

If op is a Recordset, the result is a Recordset with the same Key Components and Records as op, whose Fact Component is the extracted Integer value (or null). If op is a Scalar, the result is an Integer Scalar.

docs.title: 10.2.1.4 Common Semantics
docs.text: Week numbers follow the ISO-8601 convention (week 1 is the week containing the first Thursday of the year; weeks range 1..53).

docs.title: 10.2.1.5 Common Null Semantics

docs.title: 10.2.1.6 Common Additional Constraints

docs.title: 10.2.1.7 Common Behaviour
docs.text:
• Unary Operators' standard behaviour.
  • If op is a Recordset, the Operator is applied to every Record's Fact value (a Date) and the result is a Recordset with the same Key Components and Records whose Fact Component is the extracted Integer. Attribute Components are not propagated.

{vmaturity}

id f L001 #2024-03-15# L002 #2025-06-30# L003 #2023-12-31#

year({vmaturity}) returns:

docs.title: 10.3.1 Syntax
docs.text: date( year, month, day )

docs.title: 10.3.2 Input Parameters
docs.text:
year: rset <int> | scal <int>

month: rset <int> | scal <int>

day: rset <int> | scal <int>

docs.title: 10.3.3 Output
docs.text: rset <date> | scal <date>

docs.title: 10.3.4 Semantics
docs.text:
Builds a Date (notation #YYYY-MM-DD#, see §2.4.2) from the three Integer parts.

This Operator is the sanctioned path to obtain a Date from Integers: the casting table in §2.3.2 marks Integer → Date as Not possible.

docs.title: 10.3.5 Additional Constraints
docs.text:
• year, month and day must be of Integer type.
  • Any combination of Scalar and Recordset operands is allowed, provided the Recordset operands satisfy the constraints in §2.2 Binary Operators, generalised to three operands: Recordset operands must share Key Components (or one's Key Components must be a superset of the others'), and Standard Keys must contain matching values.

docs.title: 10.3.6 Behaviour
docs.text:
• Binary Operators' standard behaviour, generalised to three operands.
  • If all three operands are Scalars, the result is a Scalar Date built from the three values.
  • If any operand is a Recordset, the result is a Recordset whose Key Components are the common Key Components of the Recordset operands (or those of the Reference Recordset if one's Keys are a superset of the others'), and whose Fact Component is the Date built per Record. Per-Record construction uses the inner join of the Recordset operands on their common Key Components; Scalar operands are broadcast to every Record. Attribute Components are not propagated.
  • If any of year, month or day is null on a given Record (or Scalar), the resulting Date for that Record (or Scalar) is null.
  • If the three values do not form a valid calendar date — month outside 1..12, or day outside the valid range for that month and year (accounting for leap years; e.g. date(2025, 2, 30)) — the resulting Date is null.

docs.title: 10.3.7 Examples
docs.text:
• date(2025, 12, 31) → #2025-12-31#
  • date(2024, 2, 29) → #2024-02-29# (2024 is a leap year)
  • date(2025, 2, 30) → null (not a valid date)
  • date(2025, 13, 1) → null (month out of range)
  • date(null, 1, 1) → null
  • date(year(refPeriod), 1, 1) — first day of each Record's reference year (round-trips with the extraction family of §10.2).

Considering the following Recordsets (selections of three Variables sharing the same Key Components):

{vyyyy}

id f A 2024 B 2025

{vmm}

id f A 2 B 12

{vdd}

id f A 29 B 31

date({vyyyy}, {vmm}, {vdd}) returns:

id f A #2024-02-29# B #2025-12-31#

Mixing Recordsets and Scalars is also allowed; the Scalar is broadcast. date({vyyyy}, 1, 1) returns:

id f A #2024-01-01# B #2025-01-01#

docs.title: 10.4.1 Syntax
docs.text: annualise( op, fyEnd, var )

docs.title: 10.4.2 Input Parameters
docs.text:
op: rset <num> | scal <num>

fyEnd: scal <int>

var: scal <prop>

docs.title: 10.4.3 Output
docs.text: rset <num> | scal <num>

docs.title: 10.4.4 Semantics
docs.text:
Annualise scales each numeric value in op up to its full-year equivalent based on where the Record's reference month sits within the surrounding financial year. The scaling is computed in whole months: a financial year always spans 12 months, and each value is grossed up by the ratio of 12 to the number of months elapsed since the start of the financial year.

The relevant quantities are:

flowchart LR subgraph FY["Financial Year — 12 months"] direction LR fyStart["fyStart (month after fyEnd)"] -- "elapsed months" --> m["reference month m"] m -- "remaining months" --> fyEndMonth["fyEnd"] end

where, for each Record:

  • m is the month of the Record's reference date — the month component (1..12) of the value of var for that Record. Only the month is used; the day within the month does not affect the result.
  • fyEnd is the month code of the last month of the financial year: an integer in 1..12 (e.g., 12 for a calendar financial year, 3 for a financial year ending in March).
  • elapsed is the number of months from the start of the financial year up to and including month m. The financial year starts in the month following fyEnd, so:
elapsed = 12 - (fyEnd - m)   if fyEnd >= m
elapsed = m - fyEnd          if fyEnd <  m

The annualised value for each Record is then:

annualised = value * (12 / elapsed)

docs.title: 10.4.5 Additional Constraints
docs.text:
• fyEnd must be an integer in the range 1..12. Any other value raises a runtime error.
  • var must be provided, must belong to op, as a Key or Attribute Component of the Recordset, and must be of Date type. Only its month component is used.
  • The Fact Component of op (or the Scalar's value) must be numeric.
  • If the reference date for a Record is null, the annualised value for that Record is null. .

docs.title: 10.4.6 Behaviour
docs.text: Returns a Recordset (or Scalar) with the same Structure and number of Records as op. The Fact Component of each Record is replaced by its annualised value, computed independently per Record. Key and Attribute Components are preserved unchanged.

docs.title: 10.4.7 Examples
docs.text:
Considering the following Recordset, generated from the selection {tP01, r010, c010} and reporting partial-year balances at different cut-off dates within a calendar financial year:

refPeriod f 2022-03-31 100 2022-06-30 250 2022-09-30 400 2022-12-31 600

annualise({tP01, r010, c010}, 12, refPeriod) — calendar financial year (ends in December) — returns:

refPeriod f 2022-03-31 400.00 2022-06-30 500.00 2022-09-30 533.33 2022-12-31 600.00

(For the first Record: m = 3, fyEnd = 12, and since fyEnd >= m, elapsed = 12 - (12 - 3) = 3 months, so 100 * 12 / 3 = 400.00. The last Record sits in month fyEnd, so elapsed = 12 and the value is unchanged.)

annualise({tP01, r010, c010}, 3, refPeriod) — financial year ending in March — returns:

refPeriod f 2022-03-31 100.00 2022-06-30 1000.00 2022-09-30 800.00 2022-12-31 800.00

(For 2022-03-31: m = 3, fyEnd = 3, and since fyEnd >= m, elapsed = 12 - (3 - 3) = 12 months — it sits in month fyEnd, so the value is unchanged. For 2022-06-30: m = 6, fyEnd = 3, and since fyEnd < m, elapsed = 6 - 3 = 3 months, so 250 * 12 / 3 = 1000.00. Note: with fyEnd = 3, the first cut-off belongs to a different financial year from the other three.)

For a Scalar operand, the contextual refPeriod of the instance (always latent — see §2.2.3.1.4) is passed explicitly as var:

annualise({tP01, r010, c010}, 12, refPeriod)

docs.title: 11 Clause Operators
docs.text: Clause Operators serve to perform operations on the Components of Recordsets. Which roles of Component (Key, Fact or Attribute) each clause Operator accepts is specified in its Additional Constraints: where may reference any of them, while rename, get and sub apply only to Key and, where indicated, Attribute Components. Use of clause Operators with Standard Key Components ("r", "c" or "s") is not allowed.

docs.title: 11.1.1 Syntax
docs.text: op [where condition ]

docs.title: 11.1.2 Input Parameters
docs.text:
op: rset <*>

condition: expression <boo>

docs.title: 11.1.3 Output
docs.text: rset <*>

docs.title: 11.1.4 Semantics
docs.text: Filters a Recordset based on the values of its Components.

docs.title: 11.1.5 Additional Constraints
docs.text:
Condition must be a Boolean expression using as input Components of op — any of its DPM Key Components, its Fact Component, or its Attribute Components. The contextual Components are latent in every Recordset and may therefore always be referenced: refPeriod and entityID (§2.2.3.1.4), and the contextual Attribute Components (§2.2.3.3.1).

Standard Key Components ("r", "c" or "s") cannot be referenced in the condition.

docs.title: 11.1.6 Behaviour
docs.text: Returns a Recordset with the same data structure as the input Operand, and with the Records resulting from the evaluation of the filtering condition. When the condition evaluates to true, the Record is kept, otherwise (including null), the Record is not kept.

docs.title: 11.1.7 Examples
docs.text:
Considering the following Recordset, generated from the selection {tT1, r010-020}:

refPeriod r CNT f 2022Q1 010 ES 100 2022Q1 010 PT 200 2022Q1 010 DE 300 2022Q1 010 IT 400 2022Q2 020 ES 500 2022Q2 020 PT 600 2022Q2 020 DE 700 2022Q2 020 800

{tT1, r010-020}[where CNT in {"ES", "PT"}] returns:

refPeriod r CNT f 2022Q1 010 ES 100 2022Q1 010 PT 200 2022Q2 020 ES 500 2022Q2 020 PT 600

{tT1, r010-020}[where f != 0] keeps only the Records with a non-zero Fact value. In the example above, all the Records are kept, as none of them has a zero or null Fact.

{tT1, r010-020}[where f > 300 and CNT = "PT"] combines Fact and Key filtering, and returns:

refPeriod r CNT f 2022Q2 020 PT 600

{tT1, r010-020}[where not isnull(f)] keeps only the Records with a non-null Fact value.

docs.title: 11.2.1 Syntax
docs.text: op [rename compFrom to compTo {, compFrom to compTo} ]*

docs.title: 11.2.2 Input Parameters
docs.text:
op: rset <*>

compFrom: scal <prop>

compTo: scal <prop>

docs.title: 11.2.3 Output
docs.text: rset <*>

docs.title: 11.2.4 Semantics
docs.text: Changes the name of a Component.

docs.title: 11.2.5 Additional Constraints
docs.text:
compFrom must belong to op.

compFrom may refer to a DPM Key Component or to an Attribute Component, including a contextual Attribute Component (§2.2.3.3.1), which is latent in every Recordset and therefore always belongs to op. It cannot refer to a Standard Key Component (i.e., cannot refer to row, column or sheet), nor to the Fact Component (the name of the Fact Component is always "f", as specified in §2.2.3.2).

compTo name cannot be already used in op.

compTo name cannot be the name of a standard Key Component ("r", "c" or "s"), nor the name of a contextual Component (§2.4.3), which would make the contextual Component unaddressable.

docs.title: 11.2.6 Behaviour
docs.text: Returns a Recordset with the same data structure as the input Operand, except the renamed Components, which change name. The role of each renamed Component (Key or Attribute) is preserved. All the Records are kept.

docs.title: 11.2.7 Examples
docs.text:
Considering the following Recordset, generated from the selection {tT1, r010-020}:

refPeriod r CNT f 2022Q1 010 ES 100 2022Q1 010 PT 200 2022Q1 010 DE 300 2022Q1 010 IT 400 2022Q2 020 ES 500 2022Q2 020 PT 600 2022Q2 020 DE 700 2022Q2 020 800

{tT1, r010-020}[rename CNT to country] returns:

refPeriod r country f 2022Q1 010 ES 100 2022Q1 010 PT 200 2022Q1 010 DE 300 2022Q1 010 IT 400 2022Q2 020 ES 500 2022Q2 020 PT 600 2022Q2 020 DE 700 2022Q2 020 800

Considering now a Recordset with an Attribute Component "p" (precision), generated from the selection {tT2, r010}:

refPeriod CNT f p 2022Q1 ES 100 1 2022Q1 PT 200 0

{tT2, r010}[rename p to precision] renames the Attribute Component, and returns:

refPeriod CNT f precision 2022Q1 ES 100 1 2022Q1 PT 200 0

docs.title: 11.3.1 Syntax
docs.text: op [get component ]

docs.title: 11.3.2 Input Parameters
docs.text:
op: rset <*>

component: scal <prop>

docs.title: 11.3.3 Output
docs.text: rset <*>

docs.title: 11.3.4 Semantics
docs.text: Returns a Recordset where the Fact is the value of one of the Key or Attribute Components.

docs.title: 11.3.5 Additional Constraints
docs.text:
component must belong to op.

component may refer to a DPM Key Component or to an Attribute Component, including a contextual Attribute Component (§2.2.3.3.1), which is latent in every Recordset and therefore always belongs to op. It cannot refer to a Standard Key Component (i.e., cannot refer to row, column or sheet), nor to the Fact Component (the operation would have no effect).

docs.title: 11.3.6 Behaviour
docs.text:
Returns a Recordset with the same data structure as the input Operand. The Fact values the Records are substituted for the value of the selected Component. The Data Type of the Fact Component of the result is the Data Type of the selected Component.

Records with null Fact value will be omitted.

docs.title: 11.3.7 Examples
docs.text:
Considering the following Recordset, generated from the selection {tT1, r010-020}:

refPeriod r CNT f 2022Q1 010 ES 100 2022Q1 010 PT 200 2022Q1 010 DE 300 2022Q1 010 IT 400 2022Q2 020 ES 500 2022Q2 020 PT 600 2022Q2 020 DE 700 2022Q2 020 IT 800

{tT1, r010-020}[get CNT] returns:

refPeriod r CNT f 2022Q1 010 ES ES 2022Q1 010 PT PT 2022Q1 010 DE DE 2022Q1 010 IT IT 2022Q2 020 ES ES 2022Q2 020 PT PT 2022Q2 020 DE DE 2022Q2 020 IT IT

Considering now a Recordset with an Attribute Component "p" (precision), generated from the selection {tT2, r010}:

refPeriod CNT f p 2022Q1 ES 100 1 2022Q1 PT 200 0

{tT2, r010}[get p] promotes the value of the Attribute Component into the Fact Component, so that it can be further aggregated or compared, and returns:

refPeriod CNT f p 2022Q1 ES 1 1 2022Q1 PT 0 0

docs.title: 11.4.1 Syntax
docs.text: op [sub key_component = value {, key_component = value} ]*

docs.title: 11.4.2 Input Parameters
docs.text:
op: rset <*>

key_component: scal <prop>

The right-hand side value accepts three forms:

Form Syntax Description Literal A scalar literal value A constant of a basic type (String, Number, Boolean, Date, etc.) written directly in the expression. Select { selectOperand } A selection expression that resolves to a Scalar value (e.g., a single-cell table selection or a Variable reference). Item reference [ dimension : member ] A dimension member reference using the dimension:member notation.

docs.title: 11.4.3 Output
docs.text: rset | scal <*>

docs.title: 11.4.4 Semantics
docs.text: Filters a Recordset based on the value of a Key Component, and then drops the Key Component. If all Key Components are substituted, the result is a Scalar.

docs.title: 11.4.5 Additional Constraints
docs.text:
key_component must belong to op, and must be a DPM Key Component. It cannot refer to the Fact Component (substituting it would leave the Recordset without a value) nor to an Attribute Component.

The value needs to have the same Data type as the key_component.

docs.title: 11.4.6 Behaviour
docs.text: Returns a Recordset with the same data structure as the input Operand, except the Key Components dropped, and with the Records resulting from the evaluation of the filtering condition. When the condition evaluates to true, the Record is kept, otherwise (including null), the Record is not kept. If no Key Components remain after the substitution, the result is a Scalar.

docs.title: 11.4.7 Examples
docs.text:
Considering the following Recordset, generated from the selection {tT1, r010-020}:

refPeriod r CNT f 2022Q1 010 ES 100 2022Q1 010 PT 200 2022Q1 010 DE 300 2022Q1 010 IT 400 2022Q2 020 ES 500 2022Q2 020 PT 600 2022Q2 020 DE 700 2022Q2 020 800

Form 1 — Literal

{tT1, r010-020}[sub CNT = "PT"] returns:

refPeriod r f 2022Q1 010 200 2022Q2 020 600

Form 2 — Select

Where {vCountry} is a Variable that resolves to the String "ES":

{tT1, r010-020}[sub CNT = {vCountry}] returns:

refPeriod r f 2022Q1 010 100 2022Q2 020 500

Form 3 — Item reference

{tT1, r010-020}[sub CNT = [CNT:ES]] returns:

refPeriod r f 2022Q1 010 100 2022Q2 020 500

docs.title: 12 Assignment Operators
docs.text: Assignment Operators serve to assign the result of an operation to a name or to a DPM Variable.

docs.title: 12.1.1 Syntax
docs.text: name := op

docs.title: 12.1.2 Input Parameters
docs.text:
name: the name assigned to the result

op: the operand, which can be any dpm-xl expression

docs.title: 12.1.3 Output
docs.text: Assigns the name to the op.

docs.title: 12.1.4 Semantics
docs.text: Allows a DPM-XL operation to use the result of another operation as input. By assigning a name to the result of an operation, this result can be selected using the selection operator.

docs.title: 12.1.5 Additional Constraints
docs.text: name must be a valid temporary identifier as defined in the grammar.

docs.title: 12.1.6 Behaviour
docs.text: The value of the Operand op is assigned the name name, which is non-persistent and therefore is not stored. The operand op can be obtained through an expression as complex as needed (for example: op1 := {tT1, r010-020} * 10).

docs.title: 12.2.1 Syntax
docs.text: var_sel <- op

docs.title: 12.2.2 Input Parameters
docs.text:
var_sel: a selection operator with the output variable

op: the operand, which can be any dpm-xl expression

docs.title: 12.2.3 Output
docs.text: Assigns the result of op to the var_sel.

docs.title: 12.2.4 Semantics
docs.text: Links the calculation of a DPM Variable to an expression.

docs.title: 12.2.5 Additional Constraints
docs.text: var_sel is a selection Operator that refers to a Variable or set of Variables that are defined in the DPM. The resulting Structure in op needs to be equal to the Structure of var_sel.

docs.title: 12.2.6 Behaviour
docs.text: The value of the Operand op is assigned the Variables selected in var_sel, with the objective of storing the result. The operand op can be obtained through an expression as complex as needed (for example: {tOT1, r010-020} <- {tT1, r010-020} * 10).

docs.title: 13 Set Operators
docs.text:
Set Operators construct and combine Scalar Sets (see §2.2.2). A Scalar Set is an unordered, duplicate-free collection of Scalar values that share a single Data Type. Until now, Scalar Sets could only be written as literals ({v1, v2, ...}, or {} for the empty set) or obtained from a Subcategory, and were consumed only by the in Operator (§5.8). The Operators in this section make Scalar Sets first-class:

  • set_of derives a Scalar Set from the Fact Component of a Recordset.
  • union, intersect, setdiff and symdiff combine Scalar Sets.

The cardinality of a Scalar Set (its number of distinct elements) is obtained with the count Operator (§7.3), which accepts a scalar_set in addition to a Recordset.

Each combining Operator (union, intersect, setdiff, symdiff) is illustrated below with a Venn diagram of two example sets, set 1 = {1, 2, 3} and set 2 = {3, 4, 5}, in which the shaded region marks the elements that end up in the result.

A set-valued expression — a literal, a Subcategory, a set-* Parameter, or the result of any Operator in this section — may appear as the right-hand side of in, as the Operand of count, as an Operand of the binary and variadic set Operators (so they nest freely, e.g. union(set_of(A), setdiff(B, C))), and as an Operand of the equality Operators = and != (see Set Equality).

Where a set Operand is written as a Recordset or Subcategory selection, it is implicitly read as the Scalar Set of its values — equivalent to wrapping it in set_of (§13.2). So union({tC_28.00, c020}[get qINC], {tC_29.00, c0030}[get qINC]) is accepted directly, without an explicit set_of around each selection.

These are semantic rules, not syntactic ones: the grammar accepts an ordinary expression in every set position, and semantic analysis is responsible for the type restrictions. In particular, set-valued expressions are not Scalars or Recordsets, so — apart from set equality — they cannot be combined with scalar/recordset Operators: arithmetic and the ordering comparisons (<, >, <=, >=) are not defined on Scalar Sets, and a comparison such as {c020} = setdiff(A, B) (a Recordset against a Scalar Set) is rejected by semantic analysis even though it parses.

docs.title: 13.1.1 Syntax
docs.text: setOperator ( s1, s2 {, s3}* )

docs.title: 13.1.2 Input Parameters
docs.text: s1, s2, ...: scalar_set <> | subcategory | rset <>

docs.title: 13.1.3 Output
docs.text: scalar_set <T>

docs.title: 13.1.4 Semantics
docs.text: The binary and variadic set Operators combine their Operands into a new Scalar Set. Membership is decided element-wise using the equality Operator (=), so two elements are "the same" exactly when they compare equal under =; for intervals, this inherits the interval semantics of = (see §5.2). The result is always a Scalar Set: unordered and duplicate-free.

docs.title: 13.1.5 Additional Constraints
docs.text:
• All elements within a Scalar Set must share a single Data Type, considering implicit casting.
  • For a binary or variadic set Operator, the Operands must have compatible element Data Types. The element Data Type of the result is the maximum common Data Type of the Operands, determined by the implicit casting hierarchy (§2.3.2) — e.g. combining an Integer set with a Number set yields a Number set.
  • A Subcategory Operand is implicitly treated as a Scalar Set of its member items, consistently with the in Operator (§5.8).
  • A Recordset Operand is implicitly treated as the Scalar Set of its Fact Component values, exactly as if wrapped in set_of (§13.2). To take the set of a Key or Attribute Component instead, move it into the Fact first with the get clause — e.g. union(A[get CNT], B[get CNT]).
  • null is not a valid set element. Set Operators never introduce null; any null arising at construction time (e.g. from set_of) is dropped.

docs.title: 13.1.6 Behaviour
docs.text: Set Operators operate purely on the values of their Operands; they do not carry Key or Attribute Components, since their result is a Scalar Set, not a Recordset. The result contains each distinct value at most once.

docs.title: 13.2.1 Syntax
docs.text: set_of( op )

docs.title: 13.2.2 Input Parameters
docs.text: op: rset <*>

docs.title: 13.2.3 Output
docs.text: scalar_set <T> — where T is the Data Type of the Fact Component of op.

docs.title: 13.2.4 Semantics
docs.text:
Returns the Scalar Set of distinct, non-null values taken by the Fact Component across the Records of op.

To obtain the set of values of a Key or Attribute Component, first move that Component into the Fact with the get clause Operator, then apply set_of — e.g. set_of(op[get CNT]).

docs.title: 13.2.5 Additional Constraints
docs.text: None.

docs.title: 13.2.6 Behaviour
docs.text: Each Record of op contributes its Fact value. Duplicate values collapse to a single element, and Records whose Fact value is null contribute nothing. The result is a Scalar Set whose element Data Type is that of the Fact Component of op.

docs.title: 13.2.7 Examples
docs.text:
Considering the following Recordset, generated from the selection {tT1, r010-020}:

refPeriod r CNT f 2022Q1 010 ES 100 2022Q1 010 PT 200 2022Q1 010 DE 300 2022Q1 010 IT 400 2022Q2 020 ES 500 2022Q2 020 PT 600 2022Q2 020 DE 700 2022Q2 020 IT 800

set_of({tT1, r010-020}) results in {100, 200, 300, 400, 500, 600, 700, 800} — the distinct Fact values.

set_of({tT1, r010-020}[get CNT]) results in {"ES", "PT", "DE", "IT"} — the get clause first moves CNT into the Fact.

docs.title: 13.3.1 Syntax
docs.text: union( s1, s2 {, s3}* )

docs.title: 13.3.2 Input Parameters
docs.text: s1, s2, ...: scalar_set <*> | subcategory

docs.title: 13.3.3 Output
docs.text: scalar_set <T>

docs.title: 13.3.4 Semantics
docs.text: Returns the Scalar Set of elements present in any of the Operands. union accepts two or more Operands.

docs.title: 13.3.5 Additional Constraints
docs.text: • Set Operators' general behaviour.

docs.title: 13.3.6 Behaviour
docs.text: • Set Operators' general behaviour.

docs.title: 13.3.7 Examples
docs.text:
• union({1, 2, 3}, {3, 4, 5}) results in {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}.
  • union({1}, {2}, {3}) results in {1, 2, 3}.

docs.title: 13.4.1 Syntax
docs.text: intersect( s1, s2 {, s3}* )

docs.title: 13.4.2 Input Parameters
docs.text: s1, s2, ...: scalar_set <*> | subcategory

docs.title: 13.4.3 Output
docs.text: scalar_set <T>

docs.title: 13.4.4 Semantics
docs.text: Returns the Scalar Set of elements present in all of the Operands. intersect accepts two or more Operands.

docs.title: 13.4.5 Additional Constraints
docs.text: • Set Operators' general behaviour.

docs.title: 13.4.6 Behaviour
docs.text: • Set Operators' general behaviour.

docs.title: 13.4.7 Examples
docs.text:
• intersect({1, 2, 3}, {3, 4, 5}) results in {3}.
  • intersect({1, 2, 3}, {2, 3, 4}, {3, 4, 5}) results in {3}.

docs.title: 13.5.1 Syntax
docs.text: setdiff( s1, s2 )

docs.title: 13.5.2 Input Parameters
docs.text: s1, s2: scalar_set <*> | subcategory

docs.title: 13.5.3 Output
docs.text: scalar_set <T>

docs.title: 13.5.4 Semantics
docs.text: Returns the Scalar Set of elements in s1 that are not in s2. setdiff is binary and not symmetric: the order of the Operands matters.

docs.title: 13.5.5 Additional Constraints
docs.text: • Set Operators' general behaviour.

docs.title: 13.5.6 Behaviour
docs.text: • Set Operators' general behaviour.

docs.title: 13.5.7 Examples
docs.text:
• setdiff({1, 2, 3}, {3, 4, 5}) results in {1, 2}.
  • setdiff({3, 4, 5}, {1, 2, 3}) results in {4, 5}.

docs.title: 13.6.1 Syntax
docs.text: symdiff( s1, s2 )

docs.title: 13.6.2 Input Parameters
docs.text: s1, s2: scalar_set <*> | subcategory

docs.title: 13.6.3 Output
docs.text: scalar_set <T>

docs.title: 13.6.4 Semantics
docs.text: Returns the Scalar Set of elements in exactly one of s1 or s2 — equivalently, setdiff(union(s1, s2), intersect(s1, s2)). symdiff is binary and symmetric.

docs.title: 13.6.5 Additional Constraints
docs.text: • Set Operators' general behaviour.

docs.title: 13.6.6 Behaviour
docs.text: • Set Operators' general behaviour.

docs.title: 13.6.7 Examples
docs.text:
• symdiff({1, 2, 3}, {3, 4, 5}) results in {1, 2, 4, 5}.
  • symdiff({1, 2}, {1, 2}) results in {} (the empty set).

docs.title: 13.7 Set Equality (=, !=)
docs.text: The equality Operators = and != accept two set-valued Operands and compare them as Scalar Sets, returning a single Boolean. This is the only comparison defined on Scalar Sets: the ordering Operators (<, >, <=, >=) and the arithmetic Operators are not defined on sets.

docs.title: 13.7.2 Input Parameters
docs.text: s1, s2: scalar_set <*> | subcategory

docs.title: 13.7.3 Output
docs.text: scal <boo>

docs.title: 13.7.4 Semantics
docs.text:
s1 = s2 returns true when the two Scalar Sets contain exactly the same elements — every element of s1 is in s2 and every element of s2 is in s1 — and false otherwise. s1 != s2 is its negation. Membership is decided with the same element-wise equality as the other set Operators (§13.1.4); order and duplicates are irrelevant, since both Operands are Scalar Sets.

The empty set is written {}. Comparing against it tests emptiness: s = {} is true exactly when s has no elements.

docs.title: 13.7.5 Additional Constraints
docs.text:
• The two Operands must have compatible element Data Types, following the same rule as the combining set Operators (§13.1.5).
  • Set equality applies when both Operands are set-valued (a set literal, a set Operator result, a set-* Parameter, or a Subcategory). When both Operands are instead Scalars or Recordsets, = and != denote the ordinary comparison (§5.2, §5.3); a comparison that mixes a Scalar Set with a Scalar or Recordset is rejected by semantic analysis. The grammar does not distinguish these cases — the choice is made from the Operand types. For instance, {c020} = {c030} is a Recordset comparison when c020/c030 are ordinary Recordset selections; wrap an Operand in set_of (or use a set literal or set Operator) to make the comparison set-valued.

docs.title: 13.7.6 Behaviour
docs.text: Both Operands are evaluated to Scalar Sets and compared by value; the result is a single Boolean Scalar.

docs.title: 13.7.7 Examples
docs.text:
• {1, 2, 3} = {3, 2, 1} results in true (order does not matter).
  • {1, 2} = {1, 2, 3} results in false.
  • symdiff({1, 2}, {1, 2}) = {} results in true (equal sets have an empty symmetric difference).
  • setdiff({tT1, r010}[get CNT], {tT2, r020}[get CNT]) = {} results in true when every CNT value of the first selection also appears in the second — i.e. the first set is a subset of the second. Each selection is coerced to its Scalar Set (§13.1.5), so no explicit set_of is needed.

docs.title: 1.1 Scope
docs.text:
This part specifies the DPM-XL Script Document: a JSON serialisation of the complete set of DPM-XL Operations applicable to one module version, together with the metadata required to evaluate them.

A Script Document is the deliverable that a DPM authority may publish and that a validation engine is expected to be able to consume. It is generated from the DPM-ML metamodel (see Information Model §5 DPM-ML) and is intended to be the only input an engine needs, besides the reported data itself.

This part is normative. It occupies the same position as the Grammar: where the grammar defines what a well-formed DPM-XL expression looks like, this part defines what an engine actually receives and how it must be interpreted.

What this part specifies is an encoding, and only an encoding. Three things are therefore outside its scope, and are named here because each has at some point been mistaken for its business:

  • What an expression means. The semantics of every Operator belong to the Operators part and the Information Model. This part encodes Operations whose meaning is settled elsewhere; where it appears to constrain meaning, it is citing those parts, not adding to them.
  • Whether an expression is meaningful. Type agreement between operands, the admissibility of an argument to an Operator, and every other question of semantic analysis are settled before a Script Document is produced. A Script Document is the output of a pipeline whose semantic analysis has already passed, so this part neither restates those rules nor asks a Consumer to re-derive them.
  • What a Consumer produces. The result of evaluating a document — its outcome categories, counts, messages and report structure — is implementation-specific by design. What is standardised here is the input an engine receives, so that independent engines consume the same documents; what they emit is their own concern.

The structural validation rules of §5.3 mark the boundary precisely: each is decidable from the document alone, without knowing what any Operator means, without a DPM database, and without an instance.

docs.title: 1.2 Why a Serialised Script Format
docs.text:
A DPM-XL expression is not self-contained. The expression

with {tC_28.00, default: 0, interval: true}: {c040} >= {c050}

denotes nothing until C_28.00 is resolved to a table version, c040 and c050 to sets of Variables, and the enclosing with context to a fallback value and an interval-arithmetics setting. All of that lives in the DPM. Publishing expression strings alone would therefore oblige every engine to embed a copy of the DPM database and reimplement its resolution logic.

The Script Document exists to remove that obligation. Five properties motivate it:

  1. Self-containment. Every Operand carries its own fully resolved coordinates and Variable identifiers, including data types. Evaluation requires no lookup outside the document.
  2. Decoupling. Engines should be able to run the validations without needing to access the DPM database.
  3. Determinism. Range expansion, with propagation and Operand index assignment are performed once, by the authority. Two conforming engines therefore combine exactly the same Variables in exactly the same pairs.
  4. Auditability. Because the expansion is published rather than recomputed, a validation result can be traced to a specific Variable set, and two releases of the same module can be diffed mechanically.
  5. Deployment. One file per module version, transferable and cacheable, with no database dependency.

docs.title: 1.3 Relationship to the Other Parts of This Specification
docs.text:
Part Governs Information Model The data structures DPM-XL operates on: Recordsets, Records, Components, Variables, null treatment. Operators The semantics of each Operator — signature, output type, behaviour. Authoritative for meaning. Grammar The concrete surface syntax of DPM-XL expressions. Script Format (this part) The serialised, resolved form in which Operations are published and consumed. Authoritative for encoding.

This part defines no semantics of its own. For every Operator it specifies the encoding and refers to the Operators part for behaviour. Where an encoding rule here appears to imply a semantics that the Operators part contradicts, the Operators part prevails.

docs.title: 1.4 Conformance
docs.text:
The key words MUST, MUST NOT, REQUIRED, SHALL, SHALL NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT, RECOMMENDED, MAY and OPTIONAL are to be interpreted as described in RFC 2119.

Two conformance targets are defined:

  • A conforming Producer is a process that emits Script Documents. It MUST satisfy every requirement in §5.1 and MUST emit only documents that satisfy the structural validation rules of §5.3.
  • A conforming Consumer is a process that reads Script Documents and evaluates the Operations they contain. It MUST satisfy every requirement in §5.2.

A Script Document is valid if and only if it satisfies every rule in §5.3.

Encoding, media type and file naming are specified in §3.1.

docs.title: 1.5 Terminology
docs.text:
Term Definition Script Document A single JSON document conforming to this part. Module Object The value of the single member of the root object; carries all content for one module version (§3.2). Operation Object The serialised form of one OperationVersion for this module version (§3.10). Node One JSON object in an abstract syntax tree, discriminated by class_name (§4.1). Operand Node A Node denoting data, a literal or a named value rather than an Operator: VarID, Constant, Scalar, Set, Dimension, ParameterRef, PreconditionItem. Operator Node Any Node that is not an Operand Node. This covers the Operator classes proper, the parenthesised expression ParExpr (§4.10), and the two clause classes GroupingClause and AnalyticClause (§4.19, §4.20). The "Kind" column of §4.1.2 names these three groups separately, for orientation; wherever this part says Operator Node it means the whole complement of Operand Node. Datapoint Reference One entry of a VarID.data array: a Variable identifier, the resolved coordinates of the cell holding it, and a Position Index component on each axis that varies within the Operand (§4.3). Position Index The (x, y, z) triple locating a Datapoint Reference on the row, column and sheet axes of its Operand. A component is present only on an axis that varies within the Operand (§2.4). Module Parameter A named execution-time value — a Scalar or a Scalar Set — declared in parameters (§3.9) and read by a ParameterRef Node (§4.8), which carries its fallback. Resolved Said of an Operand that carries its own complete coordinates, fallback value and interval setting, independent of any enclosing lexical context (§2.3).

Throughout this part, "Variable" means a DPM Variable as defined in the Information Model, identified by its VariableID. JSON member names are written in code style; DPM-ML table and column names are written in italics.

A cross-reference of the form §X.Y always denotes a section of this part. References to other parts always name the part, as in "Operators §7" or "Information Model §5.3".

docs.title: 2 Structure and Concepts
docs.text: This chapter explains the shape of a Script Document and the five concepts needed to read one. It is expository; the normative field-by-field rules are in §3 and §4.

docs.title: 2.1 The Document at a Glance
docs.text:
A Script Document is a JSON object with exactly one member. Its name is the taxonomy module URI; its value is the Module Object.

{
  "http://www.eba.europa.eu/eu/fr/xbrl/crr/fws/corep/4.2/mod/corep_le": {

    "format_version": "1.0",            // ── identification
    "module_code": "COREP_LE",
    "module_version": "3.3.0",
    "framework_code": "COREP",
    "dpm_release":  { "release": "4.3", "publication_date": "2026-06-28" },
    "dates":        { "from": "2026-03-31", "to": null },

    "operations":   { "EGDQ_0053": { … } },  // ── the rules
    "preconditions":{ "p_395095":  { … } },

    "variables":              { "5488018": "m" },  // ── dictionaries
    "precondition_variables": { "395095": "b" },
    "tables":       { "C_28.00": { "variables": {…}, "open_keys": {…} } },
    "parameters":   { "WAIVCONS_C10": "String" },

    "dependency_information": { … },        // ── execution planning
    "dependency_modules":     { … }
  }
}

The fourteen members of the Module Object fall into four groups:

Group Members Purpose Identification format_version, module_code, module_version, framework_code, dpm_release, dates What this document is, which revision of this specification it was written to, and when it applies. Rules operations, preconditions The Operations, as resolved abstract syntax trees. Dictionaries variables, precondition_variables, tables, parameters Type and structure information for everything the rules reference, and the Module Parameters they read. Execution planning dependency_information, dependency_modules Which rules can run on a single instance, and what the others need.

docs.title: 2.2 Keying by Module URI
docs.text:
The document is keyed by the XBRL taxonomy module URI rather than by module code. This makes a Script Document addressable directly from a reported instance: an engine that has opened an instance knows its entry-point URI and can select the applicable document without consulting a code mapping. The redundant module_code and module_version members are retained for human use and for cross-checking.

The same URI serves as the key in dependency_modules, so cross-module references are expressed in exactly one namespace.

docs.title: 2.3 Concept 1 — Resolved Operands
docs.text:
In DPM-XL surface syntax a with clause factors out coordinates shared by several Operands:

with {tC_28.00, default: 0, interval: true}: {c040} >= {c050}

In a Script Document no such context exists. The with clause is pushed down into every leaf, and each VarID Node independently carries its table, its coordinates, its fallback value and its interval-arithmetics setting:

{ "class_name": "BinOp", "op": ">=",
  "left":  { "class_name": "VarID", "table": "C_28.00", "column": "040",
             "default": 0, "interval": true, "data": [ … ] },
  "right": { "class_name": "VarID", "table": "C_28.00", "column": "050",
             "default": 0, "interval": true, "data": [ … ] } }

The consequence is that the abstract syntax tree has no scoping rules. A Node can be evaluated, cached, relocated or reported on in isolation, and a Consumer needs no environment or symbol table.

docs.title: 2.4 Concept 2 — Range Expansion and Position Indices
docs.text:
Surface DPM-XL selects ranges: {c070-190}, {r*}, {(r0010, r0015)}. A Script Document contains no ranges. Every selection is expanded into an explicit list of Datapoint References in VarID.data.

Each entry of that list carries two different kinds of information, and keeping them apart is the whole of this concept:

  • Where the cell is — its row, column and sheet codes. Every entry carries these, on every axis the table version has, whatever the selection happened to fix. They identify the cell.
  • Where the cell sits in the Operand — its Position Index, the components x, y and z. These appear only on an axis that varies within the Operand. They are what aligns one Operand against another.

The VarID itself carries a third thing: the coordinate the selection pinned, if any. {tTab1, r100, c*} pins the row, so the VarID carries row: "100". Whether each entry then repeats row: "100" is a Producer's choice — both conventions are in circulation (§4.3.2) — so a Consumer reads a cell's position from its entry and falls back to the VarID for an axis the entry omits.

Consider a table Tab1 with rows 100/200/300, columns 100/200 and sheets A/B, whose cells hold the Variables shown:

Sheet A

Column 100 Column 200 Row 100 1 4 Row 200 2 5 Row 300 3 6

Sheet B

Column 100 Column 200 Row 100 7 10 Row 200 8 11 Row 300 9 12

The Operand {tTab1, r100, c*, s*} fixes the row and varies the column and sheet axes. It expands to a VarID carrying row: "100" once, and four entries indexed on y and z:

{ "class_name": "VarID", "table": "Tab1", "row": "100",
  "interval": true, "default": 0,
  "data": [
    { "y": 1, "z": 1, "row": "100", "column": "100", "sheet": "A", "datapoint": 1,  "operand_reference_id": … },
    { "y": 2, "z": 1, "row": "100", "column": "200", "sheet": "A", "datapoint": 4,  "operand_reference_id": … },
    { "y": 1, "z": 2, "row": "100", "column": "100", "sheet": "B", "datapoint": 7,  "operand_reference_id": … },
    { "y": 2, "z": 2, "row": "100", "column": "200", "sheet": "B", "datapoint": 10, "operand_reference_id": … }
  ] }

x is absent from the entries because the row axis does not vary; row is present on them all the same.

Axis assignment

x indexes rows, y indexes columns, z indexes sheets. This is normative and matches the DPM-ML OperandReference table.

A wildcard that resolves to a single code produces a fourth case, and it is the one that catches implementations out: nothing is pinned onto the VarID, and no index is emitted either, because the axis does not vary. §4.3.2 specifies all four states; the practical rule is that a Consumer MUST read an entry's position from the entry, never from the VarID.

docs.title: Positional matching
docs.text:
Position Indices are what make a resolved tree evaluable. When an Operator combines two Operands that each expand to several Datapoint References, it combines the entries that share the same Position Index, and produces one result per index. The index is therefore the format's substitute for the Key Components that would align Records in the Information Model.
